eg\) ” in the first table means not . if \(p\) is true, then \(
eg p\) must be false. here \(p\) and \(q\) stand for arbitrary propositions, such as 1+1=2 , snow is white , or the earth is flat . so if the earth is flat is true, then the earth is not flat is false. formal logic is therefore the system that tells us what the implications are if a proposition has a given truth value. in our arguments we then only need to establish the truth of one or a few propositions and can derive further truths from them by logical rules of inference. these further truths are necessarily true, provided that our premises are true. it is important here to distinguish between the validity and the soundness of an argument. an argument is valid when its conclusion follows from its premises according to the rules of logic. it is sound only when it is both valid and its premises are true. thus, the earth is flat; therefore, it is false that the earth is not flat is a valid argument, but it is not sound. the conclusion does follow according to logical rules, but the premise, namely the earth is flat , is not true. the symbol “ \(\land\) ” in the second table means and , “ \(\lor\) ” in the third table means or , and “ \(ightarrow\) ” in the fourth table means if ... then , so \(p ightarrow q\) means if \(p\) , then \(q\) . this last connective is important for the kalam, because the argument uses the inference rule called modus ponens : \(p ightarrow q\) \(p\) \(	herefore q\) the symbol “ \(	herefore\) ” means therefore . in words, the rule is: if \(p\) , then \(q\) ; \(p\) ; therefore \(q\) . we therefore only need to establish that if \(p\) is true, then \(q\) must also be true , and that \(p\) is true , and then we can infer that \(q\) is also true. in older logical notation, \(p \supset q\) is sometimes used for material implication. this should not be confused with the set-theoretic symbol for a superset. if \(p\) and \(q\) are understood as classes or sets, the corresponding set-theoretic claim to every \(p\) is a \(q\) is \(p \subseteq q\) , not \(p \supset q\) . for example, if \(p\) stands for poodles and \(q\) for dogs, then the set of poodles is a subset of the set of dogs: \(p \subseteq q\) . that expresses the same basic idea as the conditional: if something is a poodle, then it is necessarily a dog. if every dog is a mammal and poodles are a subset of dogs, then every poodle is also a mammal. premise 1: everything that begins to exist has a cause of its existence the first premise is equivalent to: if something begins to exist, then it has a cause of its existence. or, in set-theoretic language: all things that begin to exist are a subset of the things that have a cause of their existence. this premise is the less controversial of the two main premises. in everyday experience we never see an elephant simply appear in our room, or a table come into existence without a carpenter making it. still, we should consider the arguments and counterarguments. in his 1979 book the kalam cosmological argument , which grew out of his doctoral dissertation, william lane craig gives two arguments for this premise [craig 1979: pp. 141-149]. in his article in the blackwell companion to natural theology [craig moreland 2009: pp. 182-190], he gives another. the catholic philosopher professor robert c. koons of the university of texas gives a completely new argument in a lecture at his university [universityoftexas 2014], and professor alexander pruss later picks up on it on his blog [pruss 2009]. here we will present one argument inspired by dr. craig and one argument from koons. supporting argument 1: the empirical argument the first argument is an inductive argument. excursus: inductive arguments unlike deductive arguments, inductive arguments do not yield a conclusion that follows necessarily, but one that is more likely than not. deductive arguments reason from the general to the particular. if all swans have two legs, then every individual swan also has two legs. inductive arguments go in the other direction, from the particular to the general: i have seen a white swan; therefore, all swans are probably white. there are, however, black swans in australia, so the conclusion is false. this does not mean that inductive arguments are generally unreliable. inductive arguments can also be interpreted statistically, in which case every observation strengthens the force of the inductive argument. if a die is rolled once and lands on six, that is already an inductive argument that it is loaded, but a relatively weak one. every following throw that also lands on six strengthens the inductive argument that the die is loaded. the empirical argument for the premise that everything that begins to exist has a cause of its existence is a very strong inductive argument. first, no one has ever observed something simply beginning to exist without a cause. even more importantly, every time something begins to exist, we observe that there is a cause for it. the first premise probably has the greatest possible empirical support. we will now consider two counterarguments, but first we need to clarify a term. excursus: defeaters a defeater is a counterargument. defeaters can be divided into undercutting defeaters and rebutting defeaters . we will use these english terms because they are standard in the literature. an undercutting defeater only shows that an argument does not work because it has a flaw. the conclusion could still be true; it is only the argument for it that fails, and another argument might work. a rebutting defeater , by contrast, is stronger. it shows a counterexample to the conclusion of an argument and thereby shows not only that the conclusion is actually false, but also implicitly that one of the premises must be false. counterargument 1: quantum physics this is a rebutting defeater . in a subatomic vacuum, particles can indeed arise spontaneously. but spontaneous emergence is not causeless emergence. the spontaneity shows only that the cause is indeterministic, and indeterministic causes are still causes. nor is a quantum vacuum nothing , as if the particles had no cause. a quantum vacuum is a field with fluctuating energy, governed by physical laws. the spontaneous emergence of particles in this example is therefore not causeless emergence, but has the quantum vacuum as an indeterministic cause [cf. craig moreland 2009: pp. 182-183]. counterargument 2: mereological nihilism this argument is an undercutting defeater , so it is only an undercutting counterargument. mereology is a subdiscipline of metaphysics that deals with the relation between parts and wholes [stanfordencyclopedia 2]. mereological nihilism is the position that composite objects do not really exist. only fundamental particles, which are not themselves made up of smaller particles, really exist. composite objects such as tables or human beings therefore do not exist as such. our brain merely constructs these objects, whereas in themselves only their fundamental parts exist. the argument then claims that because things like tables do not really exist, we do not really observe the coming into existence of new objects. a table does not really begin to exist; rather, fundamental particles merely change their position, and the beginning to exist of a new object is only a construction of our brain. this would undercut our inductive argument. however, the argument does not work, even if we hypothetically assume that mereological nihilism is true. after all, in particle accelerators we can observe new particles beginning to exist. the previous quantum-physics objection is also a counterexample. the most that the objection from mereological nihilism can show is that, if mereological nihilism is true, then the inductive argument has fewer supporting examples. supporting argument 2: empirical skepticism the second argument for the premise that everything that begins to exist has a cause of its premise with both philosophical and scientific arguments. scientific arguments are provisional by nature and can be overtaken by new discoveries, so here we will focus on the philosophical arguments. for one of the arguments we will not use craig’s version, but a more recent version defended by koons and pruss. the basic argument will always be that the past is finite, that there is therefore a mathematically, this appears for example when we consider how a function behaves as its input grows without bound, as in \(\lim_{x 	o \infty} f(x)\) . at every particular point the function still has a finite value; we are only considering its general behavior as it grows without end. actual infinities , by contrast, concern an actually infinite number of things. in mathematics, set theory deals with such infinities. aristotle had still argued that such an actual infinity cannot exist [aristotle 1: 3.5.204b1-206a8, cited in craig moreland 2009: p. 103]. cantor’s set theory then formed a foundation for doing mathematics with actual infinities. an infinite set can be defined as any set \(m\) that has a proper subset \(n\) with the same cardinality as \(m\) . mathematically: \[ m 	ext{ actual infinite by successive addition the first supporting argument is as follows [copan craig 2017: p. 218]: a collection formed by successive addition cannot be actually infinite. the temporal sequence of past events is a collection formed by successive addition. therefore, the temporal sequence of past events cannot be actually infinite. (from 1 and 2) the relation to the second premise of the kalam is then: if the temporal sequence of past events cannot be actually infinite, then the universe began to exist. the universe began to exist. (from 3 and 4) the argument is quite intuitive: if one only ever adds \(1\) to \(1\) , no matter how often, then this operation is potentially infinite, because it comes ever closer to infinity, but it will never actually be infinite. in my opinion, however, the argument fails, because an actual infinity can be formed by successive addition. \(\aleph_0 + 1 + 1 = \aleph_0\) : here an actual infinity was formed by successive addition. it would work only if it said: successive addition starting from a finite number . but then the premise implies exactly what it is trying to prove and thus commits the logical fallacy called begging the question . supporting argument 2: absurdities of actual infinites the argument can be formulated as follows [copan craig 2017: pp. 217-218]: an actual infinite cannot exist. an infinite temporal regress of events is an actual infinite. therefore, an infinite temporal regress of events cannot exist. (from 1 and 2) the relation to the second premise of the kalam would then be: if an infinite temporal regress of events cannot exist, then the universe began to exist. the universe began to exist. (from 3 and 4) the first premise is supported by pointing to absurdities that would arise if actual infinities were possible. absurdity 1: planetary orbits this is a relatively simple absurdity. the earth takes one year to orbit the sun; mars takes approximately 687 days, almost two earth years. in the time in which mars orbits the sun once, the earth orbits it about twice. if both planets had been orbiting the sun from an infinite past, however, both would have completed the same number of orbits around the sun. this is not a strict logical contradiction, but it is at least a counterintuitive absurdity that arises if an infinite past is possible. absurdity 2: counting down what if a person had been counting down the negative numbers toward \(0\) from an infinite past? he would have to finish today, because every past day would correspond to one of the numbers \(0, -1, -2, -3\) , and so on toward negative infinity. but the question is: why did he not finish yesterday? absurdity 3: the tristram shandy paradox [oppy 2002] tristram shandy takes one year to write about one day of his life in his diary. if he had been writing his diary from an infinite past, he would always be falling behind. and yet every entry in his diary would correspond to one day of his life, so by the present moment he would have an entry for every day he has lived. but at least 364 days would have to have no diary entry, since he takes an entire year to write about one day. here we already have a more concrete contradiction. absurdity 4: an infinite deck of cards suppose we have a shuffled deck of cards in which each card bears a natural number. we can think of two paradoxical scenarios: although the deck is perfectly randomly shuffled, every card drawn is, with probability \(100\%\) , smaller than the next card drawn. two people each draw a card, and the person with the higher card wins. since no card occurs twice, exactly one person must win. but each person, after drawing his card, must assume that the other person wins. the explanation is the same in both scenarios. no matter which card is drawn, the number of larger cards is always infinitely greater than the number of smaller cards. absurdity 5: hilbert’s hotel hilbert’s hotel is a thought experiment from the mathematician david hilbert. we imagine a hotel with infinitely many rooms. all rooms are occupied. yet if a new guest arrives, every guest in room \(n\) can simply move to room \(n+1\) . because there is no last room, every current guest still receives a room, and the new guest can take room \(1\) . the hotel therefore has room for another guest even though it is completely full. it can even make room for any finite number \(k\) of new guests by moving every current guest from room \(n\) to room \(n+k\) . the thought experiment can be made still more absurd: if an infinite number of new guests arrives, every current guest can move to room \(2n\) , thereby freeing all odd-numbered rooms. we have the absurdity that the hotel is completely full and yet still has room for new guests. we have at least demonstrated that an actual infinite can lead to extremely counterintuitive absurdities. some of these absurdities could even be reformulated as explicit contradictions, though doing so would provoke deeper counterarguments that we will not address here. we still need, however, to defend the second premise: an infinite temporal regress of events is an actual infinite . to do this, we need a short excursus into the metaphysics of time. excursus: theories of time there are two major theories of time: presentism and eternalism . there is also a further theory called the growing block theory . these three theories concern the ontological status of temporal events. ontology is the study of what exists [stanfordencyclopedia 3]. it is often used in distinction from epistemology , the study of what we know and how we know it. so when we ask about the ontological status of temporal events, the question is not our subjective experience of time, but the extent to which points in time actually exist. presentism holds that only the present actually exists. the future is purely potential, and the past no longer exists. eternalism , by contrast, holds that all points in time are equally real. the present is merely a subjective construct of our mind and is no less real than a day ago or a year from now. according to the growing block theory , the present and the past are real, while only the future is purely potential and does not actually exist. sometimes presentism and eternalism are also called the a-theory and b-theory of time, in reference to the philosopher john mctaggart ellis mctaggart. for him, an a-series is a series in which events are ordered by the relations past , present , and future . a b-series , by contrast, orders events only by the relations earlier than and later than [stanfordencyclopedia 4]. the claim that “an infinite temporal regress of events constitutes an actual infinite” therefore seems straightforwardly true only under eternalism and the growing block theory. after all, under presentism the past no longer exists. dr. craig is a presentist, but he thinks that the argument also works under his theory of time. his argument is that even under presentism, actual infinities could exist in the present solely because the past is infinite. for example, if a person counted one number for every past day, then in the present the number of counted numbers would be actually infinite. this supporting argument can also be modified. alexander pruss defends a thesis called causal finitism . it is a more modest thesis. it does not claim that all actual infinities are impossible, but only that nothing can have an infinite causal past. this thesis excludes most of the absurdities as well, avoids the dispute about theories of time, and as a more modest thesis is in principle more plausible a priori . supporting argument 3: the grim messenger paradox the argument is as follows: if the past can be infinite, then a grim messenger paradox would be possible. a grim messenger paradox is impossible. therefore, the past cannot be infinite. (from 1 and 2) if the past cannot be infinite, then the universe began to exist. the universe began to exist. (from 3 and 4) the grim messenger paradox can be formulated as follows. imagine a series of people numbered from left to right by the natural numbers starting with \(1\) . they pass a sheet of paper from right to left. their only task is this: if the sheet is blank, write your number on the sheet; if a number is already written on it, pass it on unchanged. first imagine a finite number \(n\) of people. the first person to receive the sheet will be person \(n\) . he writes his number on it, and the sheet is then passed leftward until it reaches person \(1\) . when it reaches him, \(n\) will be written on the sheet. now imagine an infinite number of people. when the sheet reaches person \(1\) , what is written on it? it cannot be blank, because otherwise person \(1\) would write “1” on it. but it also cannot contain any number \(x\) , because if it did, then person \(x+1\) would already have written his number on the sheet. we therefore have a genuine logical contradiction: there must be a number on the sheet, but no number can be on the sheet. another variant is the eternal society paradox [tisthammer 2020]. in this thought experiment, a community has existed from an infinite past. the community has a website, a book, or an oral tradition recording the result of an annual ritual. the ritual, slightly modified from the source example, is this: the whole community meets in the village square and rings the church bells, but only if the bells have never been rung before. the same contradiction arises. were the bells ever rung? for every year \(x\) , the bells cannot have been rung for the first time in year \(x\) , because if they had never been rung before year \(x\) , they would already have been rung in year \(x-1\) . at the same time, they must have been rung at least once, because if they had never been rung, then they would be rung this year at the latest. these two paradoxes are examples of benardete paradoxes , named after jose benardete. in 1964, he published a series of infinity paradoxes [benardete 1965]. nicholas shackel then published an article in 2005 [shackel 2005] in which he abstracted the general form of these paradoxes from the individual thought experiments and showed exactly which conditions generate the logical contradiction. excursus: predicate logic propositional logic is not sufficient for formulating the paradox in formal logic, because the argument is stated in predicate logic. we already had a first encounter with this when defining an infinite set. predicate logic expands propositional logic by adding quantifiers. the universal quantifier \( orall\) can be translated into natural language as for all , and the existential quantifier \(\exists\) as there exists at least one . here are a few examples to make the quantifiers easier to understand: \[  orall x: human(x) ightarrow mammal(x) \] for every \(x\) : if \(x\) is a human being, then \(x\) is also a mammal. \[  orall x: pointonsphere(x) ightarrow \exists y: (pointonsphere(y) \land leftof(y,x)) \] for every \(x\) : if \(x\) is a point on a sphere, then there exists at least one \(y\) that is also a point on the sphere and is left of \(x\) . \[ isplane(p) ightarrow \exists x: (on(x,p) \land

least one possible world, then it exists or is true possibly . if it exists or is true in all possible worlds, then it exists or is true necessarily . in every possible world, \(1+1=2\) is therefore premise if the past can be infinite, then a grim messenger paradox would be possible , we must show that if it is possible in principle for the past to be infinite, then at least one possible world exists in which the grim messenger scenario exists. in his 1986 book [lewis 1986], the philosopher david lewis describes how possible worlds can be constructed. the construction criteria are called the patchwork principle . in simplified form, it says that if we have bounded spacetime regions, then we can arrange them in a new possible world, provided that the spacetime regions do not overlap and all the relevant properties of the spacetime regions are intrinsic to those regions. to use lewis’s example: if a unicorn and a dragon are each individually possible, then we can construct a possible world \(w_1\) in which both a dragon and a unicorn exist: \[ (\diamond e \land \diamond d) ightarrow \exists w_{1}: (e \in w_{1} \land d \in w_{1}) \] the condition is that the spacetime regions \(r_d\) and \(r_e\) containing the dragon and the unicorn do not overlap in \(w_1\) . all extrinsic properties of the dragon and the unicorn are not preserved in \(w_1\) . if the unicorn in its own world \(w_e\) had the property of being one of \(1000\) existing unicorns, then the patchwork principle does not allow us to assume that this property is also preserved for \(e\) in \(w_1\) . but it does not exclude that either. we could construct another possible world \(w_2\) with \(1000\) such unicorns, in which this extrinsic property would still hold. in a 2014 article [koons 2014], professor koons generalizes lewis’s binary patchwork principle into an infinite patchwork principle, \(pinf\) . in compressed form, \(pinf\) says that, under the right structural and non-overlap conditions, countably many possible spacetime regions can be jointly represented in a single possible world in such a way that each copied region exactly resembles its original region. in the same article koons argues that the relevant properties of a messenger are intrinsic to that messenger. since we know that an individual messenger is possible, because he can exist in the actual world, and since the relevant properties are intrinsic to him, \(pinf\) allows us to construct a possible world in which the grim messenger paradox exists, assuming infinite pasts are possible. we have therefore shown that the first premise, if the past can be infinite, then a grim messenger paradox would be possible , is true. we can therefore infer that the universe began to exist. schmid’s objections since on his best objection. in order not to misrepresent his position and to weigh my counterarguments against him, i was in an email exchange with him from june 3, 2024, to june 5, 2024. excursus: joe schmid joe schmid joe schmid was born in the united states in august 2000. he was raised catholic but now describes himself as agnostic [youtubefandom 1]. he is currently a doctoral student in philosophy at princeton university, and although he has not yet obtained a higher academic degree, he has repeatedly published articles in philosophical journals and has already published two books, one of them together with daniel linford through springer [josephschmid 1]. he runs a youtube channel called “majesty of reason.” the theistic philosopher dr. josh rasmussen called schmid a “young magnus carlsen of philosophy” and said, after reviewing an article by schmid, that this article would further increase schmid’s “legend status” [twitter 1]. in a 2024 article [schmid 2024-2], schmid points out that the property of being able to transmit information to another messenger is an extrinsic property of the messenger. therefore, the patchwork principle alone would not allow us to infer that a grim messenger paradox is possible merely because an arrangement of infinitely many messengers with the relevant intrinsic properties is possible in a possible world. my answer to schmid is that his criticism is basically correct, but does not change much about the actual argument. the ability to transmit information from one messenger to another is indeed not intrinsic to a messenger. nevertheless, we still have good reasons to believe that the messengers in the patched world have this property. in the unicorn example, we saw that extrinsic properties are not generally preserved, but can still be preserved accidentally. my argument for why the extrinsic property of being able to transmit information to another messenger should be preserved is as follows. suppose we have two spacetime regions \(r_1\) and \(r_2\) in the actual world, each containing a grim messenger. we can experimentally establish that communication between \(r_1\) and \(r_2\) is possible. if \(r_1\) and \(r_2\) are directly adjacent, and their duplicates \(r_1'\) and \(r_2'\) in a patched world \(w'\) are also directly adjacent, then the regions \(r_{1,2}\) and \(r'_{1,2}\) , which encompass the respective two spacetime regions, are exactly equivalent. there is therefore no reason to assume that communication between two messengers in \(r'_{1,2}\) would not be possible. if communication in \(r'_{1,2}\) is possible, then there is no reason to assume that communication between the messengers in the regions \(r_n'\) and \(r_{n+1}'\) would not also be possible, and therefore communication between all messengers in \(w'\) should be possible. thus the grim messenger paradox would be possible in \(w'\) . so even if \(pinf\) alone does not allow us to infer that the grim messenger paradox is possible, it is still an important step in constructing the possible world \(w'\) , for which we have good reasons to think that a grim messenger paradox is possible in \(w'\) . premise 4: if the universe has a cause of its existence, then god exists most arguments for god can be divided into two stages. in the first stage, it is established that something like a necessary being, a necessary explanation, or, in this case, a first cause exists. in the second stage, it is then argued that this being, explanation, or cause must be god because it must have certain classically divine properties. since we have established a first cause here, we are now in the second stage, where we argue that this cause must have certain divine attributes sufficient to conclude that it really must be god. 1st divine attribute: eternity if the cause of the universe were not outside time, then by our definition it too would begin to exist. then it too would need a cause of its existence. since this regress could not continue into an infinite past, the very first cause must be outside time. being outside time is a first classically divine attribute. 2nd divine attribute: immateriality from empirical experience we observe that matter is fundamentally in time and changeable. this indicates that the eternal and unchangeable cause cannot be material. 3rd divine attribute: power the kalam does not directly allow us to conclude that the first cause is omnipotent. but it does at least allow us to conclude that, as the cause of the entire universe and of all material temporal existence, it must be extremely powerful. 4th divine attribute: immutability and personality since time is a measure of change, a cause outside time would also be immutable. according to craig’s model of god, god is immutable only without creation and enters time with creation. but according to our definition of beginning to exist , this is not possible. so we ask: how could an atemporal cause have a temporal effect? without creation, and note that this formulation avoids the inaccurate phrase “before creation,” there are no distinct moments in the cause; it exists eternally. as an analogy, imagine a man with free will and a deterministic robot, both existing from eternity on a park bench. only the man could have been sitting from eternity and then spontaneously decide to stand up, because free will is the only cause that can bring about an effect spontaneously without prior determining circumstances [craig moreland 2009: p. 194]. craig also formulates the point this way: if the cause is sufficient to produce the effect and has been unchanged from eternity, then it should also produce the effect from eternity [craig 2002]. agent-causation , analogous to the man on the bench, frees us from this dilemma. we have therefore shown that the kalam cosmological argument leads to an immutable, extremely powerful, eternal, immaterial, and personal cause that literally created heaven and earth. this cause we call god. why the kalam cosmological argument? the kalam has been presented here in more detail than any other argument for god’s existence in this essay. the answer to joe schmid was a counterargument to a counterargument against the patchwork principle. that, in turn, was an argument for the grim messenger paradox, which was itself an argument for premise 2 of the original kalam. we are therefore four levels beneath the original syllogism. this should illustrate how deeply even one premise of an argument can be discussed. one can imagine how counterarguments to counterarguments, and supporting arguments for supporting arguments, can broaden the discussion around an initially simple argument. this is true of practically all the arguments presented here, most of which are hundreds of years old. when one first encounters good arguments for god, especially if one hears them only from theists, one can quickly become overconfident. i hope that this deep dive prevents that kind of arrogance and encourages a certain intellectual humility. it can also happen that, when one first encounters good counterarguments, one becomes very disillusioned and begins to doubt. i hope that, despite the necessary humility, this section still gives a certain confidence in the arguments, since they can withstand even the best atheist objections. the main reason i chose the kalam, however, is simply that it is a very good argument. even though we have gone very deep here, i also think it can easily be shared with ordinary people. the basic argument is very simple: everything that begins to exist has a cause of its existence. the universe began to exist. therefore, the universe has a cause of its existence. the first premise will probably be accepted by an atheist even without further argument, simply because of empirical experience. if it is nevertheless doubted, one can argue from absurdities: if things can begin to exist without a cause, why does an elephant never simply appear in a room? or, with more direct reference to koons’ argument: how would you know that you are not simply a brain that began to exist two seconds ago with false memories? for the second premise, one can cite one of the absurdities of actual infinites, or, even better, go directly to the grim messenger paradox. it is fairly vivid, and an actual logical contradiction can be established relatively easily. then one can simply ask: an individual messenger is obviously possible; if an infinite past were really possible, would this paradox not also have to be possible? at that point, one has already given an atheist very compelling reasons to believe in a cause of the universe. finally, one only needs to derive the relevant attributes of the cause in order to establish the existence of god. the arguments given here are short and intuitive, and therefore easy to explain. the argument for personality is somewhat less intuitive, but the analogy of the man on the park bench makes even that argument understandable. dr. craig is probably the best-known figure in contemporary apologetics, writing and debating both at a popular and an academic level. the kalam is his signature argument. through this combination, it has become one of the most controversially discussed arguments for god over the last several decades. it has not only withstood that pressure to this day, but has even been strengthened by further developments from pruss and koons. in addition, the argument in its basic form is memorable and largely intuitive. vivid thought experiments can usually be found for the supporting arguments as well. in my view, therefore, it has ideal conditions for successful use in apologetics, both at a lay level and at an expert level. aristotle and st. thomas aquinas’ “unmoved mover” the argument for an unmoved mover was first formulated by aristotle in book 8 of his physics [stanfordencyclopedia 5]. later, this argument was adapted by thomas aquinas. he develops it in the summa theologiae and the summa contra gentiles and makes it one of the most influential arguments for god’s existence. excursus: aristotle aristotle aristotle (384-322 bc) is considered one of the greatest and most influential philosophers who ever lived. his more than 2000-year-old arguments are still discussed today. he likely wrote around 200 works, of which about 31 survive. in his works he treated topics ranging from logic, metaphysics, philosophy of mind, ethics, political theory, aesthetics, and rhetoric to physics and biology. he was born in northeastern greece. at around the age of 17, he began studying in plato’s academy in athens. he remained there until plato’s death in 347 bc, after which he settled in asia minor. in 343 he began tutoring the thirteen-year-old son of the macedonian king, who would later become known as alexander the great. in 335 he established his own school in athens [stanfordencyclopedia 6]. besides his influence on all subsequent western philosophy, and especially on thomas aquinas, he also had a very large influence on catholic and christian philosophy and theology in general, and on the catholic understanding of god in particular. the argument is known as the argument for an unmoved mover . to understand this correctly, we need to know what aristotle and st. thomas mean by motion. we usually understand motion as a change of position in space. for aristotle, however, this is only one kind of motion. motion means change in general. once we know what aristotle means by motion, we still need to understand how aristotle understands motion, that is, change. aristotle’s analysis of change arises from his answer to parmenides. act and potency parmenides had denied that change occurs at all. his argument convinced him that change must be an illusion, because change is impossible. a cup of coffee can change, for example, by being warm at first and cold later. for parmenides, this means that coldness was first nothing and then something. but since something cannot come from nothing, the coffee cannot become cold. the change can only be illusory. his argument can be summarized as follows [feser 2014: p. 34]: change would require existence to come from non-existence. but existence cannot come from non-existence. therefore, change is impossible. aristotle has no problem either with premise 2 or with the logical inference. he rejects premise 1. to do this, he proposes an alternative analysis of change. for him there are two ways to be : potential being and actual being . this is what we call the act-potency distinction . thus the cup of coffee is initially actually warm and potentially cold, and later potentially warm and actually cold. coldness does not go from non-existence to existence, but from one kind of existence, potential being, into another kind of existence, actual being. i think most people would agree with aristotle that change is possible. but many would probably not follow his motivation for the act-potency distinction. they would probably reject parmenides’ first premise, as aristotle does, but not see the necessity of the act-potency distinction in order to refute it. another argument for the act-potency distinction another way to arrive at the act-potency distinction is to answer the question: what determines the kind of change that occurs? why does a cause \(x\) have precisely effect \(a\) on \(y\) , and not effect \(b\) ? why does the chemical reaction of two hydrogen atoms with one oxygen atom produce water and not carbon dioxide? why can clay become a cup but not a computer? the aristotelian explanation is that \(x\) has the potential for \(a\) , but not for \(b\) . one can also ask the question more generally about the explanation for regularity in nature. it is often said that the world is governed by laws of nature. but what is a law of nature? a law of nature is not a substance, not a concrete object. at most, laws of nature are abstract objects. but abstract objects have no causal power. it is not the case that every time a mass accelerates, newton’s second law appears and causes the acting force to equal the product of mass and acceleration. laws of nature are much more simply understood as generalizations of the powers of individual substances. every material object has the potency to release energy according to the product of its mass and the square of the speed of light. this explains precisely the limits of the changes that can be produced, that is, the kind of change that is possible. a further argument for the act-potency distinction here is another formulation of the dilemma, inspired by an article by thomas mclaughlin [mclaughlin 2011: p. 218]. informally, the argument runs as follows: if \(x\) is the same as \(y\) with respect to \(a\) , then \(z\) , with respect to \(a\) , can produce the same effect in \(x\) as in \(y\) . there exist at least one \(x,y,z\) , and \(a\) , such that \(x\) and \(y\) are the same in actual being with respect to \(a\) , but \(z\) produces a different effect from \(a\) in \(x\) than in \(y\) . but if \(x\) and \(y\) are the same in actual being with respect to \(a\) , and yet \(z\) produces a different effect from \(a\) in \(x\) than in \(y\) , then \(x\) and \(y\) must differ with respect to \(a\) in some way other than actual being . that other way besides actual being can be either non-being or another kind of being . it cannot be non-being . therefore, \(x\) and \(y\) differ with respect to \(a\) in another kind of being besides actual being . there exists another kind of being besides actual being . this other kind of being is potential being . from premises 1 and 2 it follows logically that there is at least one thing and at least one property for which the thing’s actual being with respect to the property is not identical to the thing with respect to that property. put differently: the actual being of a property alone does not fully explain the property in this case. what else besides actual being could explain it? it cannot be non-being , because non-existence explains nothing. so it must be another kind of being . this other kind we call potential being . now we still need to justify the two premises. the first is that if \(x\) is the same as \(y\) with respect to \(a\) , then \(z\) , with respect to \(a\) , can produce the same effect in \(x\) as in \(y\) . we justify this inductively. if both a sheet of paper ( \(x\) ) and a car ( \(y\) ) are yellow ( \(a\) ), then adding red paint ( \(z\) ) causes both to become orange. this premise seems empirically universal if the variables are described in sufficient detail. one might object as follows: a full bathtub ( \(x\) ) and a glass of water ( \(y\) ) are the same with respect to their water temperature ( \(a\) ), which is \(100^\circ c\) . but pouring in \(100 ml\) of water at \(50^\circ c\) ( \(z\) ) has different effects: the temperature in the glass falls to \(75^\circ c\) , while the temperature in the bathtub falls only to \(99.9^\circ c\) . this does not show that premise 1 is false. it shows only that the effect with respect to \(a\) was not described precisely enough. to say that the effect is a temperature drop of \(25^\circ c\) is an inadequate description. a more precise description would be that the added water lowers the water temperature by \(25^\circ c\) per \(100 ml\) of water, in which case the effect of \(z\) on \(x\) and \(y\) with respect to \(a\) is again the same. the truth of the second premise can be demonstrated with mclaughlin’s own example. a child and a donkey are exactly the same in actual being with respect to being a mathematician, because neither is actually a mathematician at all. teaching mathematics, however, has a different effect on the child than on the donkey. the explanation is that the child is not actually a mathematician, but is potentially one, whereas the donkey is neither actually nor potentially a mathematician. when mathematics is taught to the child, he changes from non-mathematician to mathematician, and this change is precisely the actualization of a potential. formulation according to thomas aquinas now that we understand change as the actualization of a potential, we can look at the syllogism of the argument for god. thomas aquinas formulates the proof with explicit reference to aristotle [aquinas 1: book i, ch. 13, 3]. the core claim is: original: alles, was bewegt wird, wird von etwas anderem bewegt. translation: whatever is moved is moved by another. thomas’ broader reasoning is that some things are evidently in motion; whatever is in motion is moved by another; and the series of movers cannot proceed to infinity. therefore we must arrive at a first unmoved mover, which we call god. the first thing to be proven, then, is that everything that changes, or is “moved,” must be changed by something else. the catholic philosopher ed feser explains this as follows [feser 2017: p. 10]. the coldness of the cup of coffee exists only potentially. potential existence cannot have effects, because it does not yet actually exist. therefore it cannot actualize itself. the potential can only be actualized by something else that already exists actually, for example the cold air around the cup. one might say that a person can actualize his own potential to walk. but this is a misunderstanding. in such a case, the potential of a whole is actualized by the actuality of a part. the person is potentially walking, and this potential is actualized by the feet, which are actually walking. we therefore get chains of actualizations of potentials. the coldness of the coffee is actualized by the cold air; the coldness of the air is actualized by the air conditioner; the air conditioner by electricity; and so on. such a chain can either end, in which case we arrive at an unmoved mover, or it can continue to infinity. since it cannot continue to infinity, there must be an unmoved mover. now we must still show that such a chain cannot proceed to infinity. thomas aquinas and aristotle argue here very differently from how we argued in the kalam. this follows from the fact that both distinguish between two kinds of causal chains: an accidentally ordered chain and an essentially ordered chain . an accidentally ordered chain could, according to thomas, be infinite. this is a chain in which the members possess their causal power in themselves and not through something else. a chain of fathers begetting sons could, according to thomas, in principle extend to infinity, because a son has the power to beget a son in himself and not by participating in the generative power of his father. an example of an essentially ordered series , by contrast, is a bridge holding up a man, who holds up a stick, which holds up a leaf. here the members do not have the power not to fall from themselves, but only by participating in another member of the chain. while a father can die and the son can still live, the bridge cannot collapse without the leaf also falling. an essentially ordered series is therefore a series in which all the members can have a property only if the chain has a first member. since a series of movers is an essentially ordered chain , the cup has coldness only through the coldness of the air and not from itself, it needs a first member and cannot proceed to infinity. we have therefore arrived at an unmoved mover: something that causes change without itself being changed. syllogism according to davies a syllogism of the argument from davies [davies 2016], cited by schmid and linford [schmid linford 2022: p. 19], runs as follows: some things are in the process of change. whatever is in the process of change is changed by something else. whatever changes something else is itself either changed or unchanged. an infinite regress of changers, each changed by another, is impossible. therefore, there is a first cause of change that is not itself in the process of change. criticism from schmid and linford schmid and linford present two problems with this syllogism. the inference to conclusion 5 holds only if (a) and (b) hold: we interpret the conclusion as saying that there is at least one first cause for at least some changes that is not itself in the process of change. premise 4 is interpreted as denying the possibility of the following conjunction: (b.i) every first member in every per se chain of change is itself changed in a way unrelated to the causality of the series for which that first member serves as endpoint; and (b.ii) every first member in every per accidens chain of change is changed in some way, whether in a per se or per accidens series. condition (a) shows that the argument does not establish a single unmoved mover who is the first cause of all change. in practice, they are saying that we cannot infer from the claim that every chain has a terminus to the claim that there is one terminus for every chain. in natural language the difference can sound almost contradictory, but it is a perfect example of why formal logic matters. if we let \(t()\) stand for terminus of and \(x\) stand for existence-chains, the invalid inference is: \[  orall x \, \exists y \, t(y,x) 
vdash \exists y \,  orall x \, t(y,x) \] the fallacy of identifying \( orall x \exists y\) with \(\exists y  orall x\) is called the quantifier shift fallacy . the standard example is this: from the statement “every human being has a mother,” it does not follow that there exists one woman who is the mother of all human beings. conclusion this argument too can be divided roughly into two stages. in the first, the existence of a first cause, here the cause of change, is established. in the second stage, it is established that this cause must be god. the problem is that aristotle’s and thomas’ arguments work only if (a) were false. since schmid and linford demonstrate that (a) is necessary for conclusion 5, it makes no sense, in my opinion, to pursue this route further. i think this way to god simply fails. we should note, however, that there are other formulations of aristotle’s argument that do not fall victim to these problems. feser, in particular, focuses in his version not on change in general, but specifically on the actualization of the potential to exist. he therefore selects one chain among the many causal chains of change and shows that the first member of this chain must be god. excursus: ed feser edward feser edward charles feser (born april 16, 1968) is an american professor of philosophy at pasadena city college in california. he has published more than ten books and many academic articles. his research interests lie especially in the philosophical subdisciplines of metaphysics, natural theology, philosophy of mind, moral philosophy, and political philosophy. feser is a traditional catholic [edfeser 2024]. he is considered one of the most influential contemporary defenders of thomistic metaphysics. in the area of arguments for god’s existence, his book five proofs of the existence of god was especially significant, partly because its arguments influenced the well-known conservative political commentator ben shapiro. we can therefore summarize as follows: a naive version of the unmoved mover argument is not sufficient to establish god’s existence. the problem is that the various chains of actualizations of potentials must each have a first member that is unmoved with respect to the property actualized in that chain, but this does not yet mean that there is exactly one entity that is the terminus of all such chains. there are, however, variants of the argument that may still work. feser’s variant is one of them. but once all the subarguments are explained, it overlaps heavily with the de ente argument, which we will analyze next. therefore we will not examine feser’s version more closely here, but will now turn to the de ente argument. the “de ente argument” of thomas aquinas the de ente argument receives its informal name from an early work of thomas aquinas called de ente et essentia (“on being and essence”). in aristotelian metaphysics there are the categories of form and matter. every substance, such as a human being, a stone, or a tree, is as a substance composed of form and matter. matter is the stuff out of which something is made, and form explains why this matter is this specific substance and not another, or why it is more than the mere sum of its particles. form and matter relate to one another as act and potency. matter as such is pure potency, capable in principle of being many things, but actually none of them. form actualizes matter into a determinate substance. thomas aquinas followed aristotelian metaphysics, but as a believing catholic he also had to integrate into his metaphysics doctrines that aristotle, as a pagan, did not have to face. he was therefore confronted with a question: if angels are immaterial, and form and matter relate to one another as act and potency, does this mean that angels are pure act without potency, and therefore the same as god? he investigates this question in de ente et essentia , and in the process develops an argument for the existence of god that does not appear among the five ways of the summa theologiae . excursus: thomas aquinas st. thomas aquinas thomas aquinas was born in 1225 near aquino, roughly halfway between rome and naples. against the wishes of his family, he entered the dominican order at the age of 19. after studying for three years in paris, he studied in 1248 under st. albert the great in cologne. albert was a leader of the movement to harmonize christian theology with arabic and greek philosophy. after receiving his doctorate, thomas taught for several years in paris [stanfordencyclopedia 7]. alongside his work as a professor, he began writing his summa theologiae . it was intended as a textbook for theology students and educated laymen. it is divided into three parts [wikipedia 1]: the existence and nature of god; the creation of the world; angels; and the nature of man. morality, legal theory, virtue, and vice. the person and work of christ, who is man’s way to god; and the sacraments. the final part remained unfinished after thomas received a revelation from god in comparison with which his whole life’s work seemed to him “like straw.” even earlier, christ had personally appeared to him and said: “you have written well of me, thomas. what reward would you have for your labor?” thomas answered: “non nisi te, domine” - “nothing but you, lord.” thomas died in 1274. the summa was completed by his students. thomas is unquestionably the most important catholic philosopher and the philosopher who has had by far the greatest influence on catholic philosophy and theology. he was canonized in 1323 and declared a doctor of the church in 1567. his traditional feast day is march 7, before it was moved to january 28. chain of participated attributes this version of the de ente argument begins with an analysis of the attributes of composite objects. these can be distinguished into two kinds: emergent attributes and participated attributes . the power to drive is an emergent attribute of a car, because none of the car’s parts, considered by itself, has this power. only when they are composed into a car does this attribute emerge. a participated attribute , by contrast, would be the red color of a brick wall. the whole wall has the attribute of being red because it participates in the red color of the individual bricks that constitute the wall. to have an emergent attribute means to have that attribute from oneself. to have a participated attribute means to have the attribute from something else. now let us consider the attribute existence . existence cannot be an emergent attribute, because the parts of a composite object must already exist in order for the composite object to exist. therefore existence must be a participated attribute. that means every composite object exists because it participates in the existence of its parts. if the parts are themselves composed of parts, the same principle applies to them. here we again have an essentially ordered series that must have a first member. the question now is what this first member could be. we know at least that it cannot have physical parts, because its parts would then come before it in the essentially ordered series. if it were physical, it could at most be a mereological atom, that is, a hypothetical, genuinely indivisible particle without physical parts. but can a mereological atom be the terminus of an essentially ordered chain in which the members have their existence by participating in the existence of the previous member of the chain? thomas would say no, because even in such a simple thing there is still composition, not from physical parts, but from metaphysical parts. the most fundamental of these is the distinction between existence and essence, that is, the distinction between that something is and what something is. this distinction is also thomas’ answer to why angels do not exist without an act-potency distinction, even though they are not composed of form and matter. essence and existence also relate to one another as potency and act. essence and existence thomas’ argument for the essence-existence distinction is that we can understand an essence without knowing whether it actually exists. for example, we can understand the essence of a phoenix as a bird that burns and then rises again from its ashes. but this tells us nothing about whether such a phoenix really exists [kerr 2015: p. 10]. for thomas, an essence is simply that which determines what a thing is. for example, the essence of a human being is to be a rational animal. if something is not an animal or is not rational, then it cannot be a human being. by contrast, being two-legged is not essential to a human being, since a human being can lose a leg without ceasing to be human. that essences exist, at least as mind-dependent sets of attributes, is obvious, because we can recognize that there are things that as such must necessarily have a certain property, for example animality in human beings. when we ask about the existence of a thing, we ask whether it is. when we ask about the essence of a thing, we ask what it is. that there really are essences is a basic condition for individual things to exist at all. when we say that \(x\) exists, \(\exists x\) , we are saying that there is a thing that is \(x\) . for anything to exist, it must be, and it must be \(x\) ; it must therefore be distinguishable from non- \(x\) . what distinguishes a thing from other things is precisely that it has an individual essence. if there were no essences, there would be no distinction between individual things that exist. we know at the very least that we exist and that there is something besides us that exists. therefore there are individual things, and therefore there must also be essences. it is also obvious that things either possess existence as an attribute or do not. now a thing could have its existence either from itself or from something else. if it has its existence from something else, then it cannot be the terminus of our essentially ordered chain. what does it mean, then, to have existence from oneself? if its existence is separate from its essence, then it cannot exist from itself. for the essence cannot actualize its own potential to exist, since it would already have to exist in order to do so. can a thing exist essentially by having existence as part of its essence? suppose a substance \(x\) had existence as part of its essence. just as a human being is a rational animal, so that rationality and animality are parts of its essence, \(a\) , \(b\) , and existence would be parts of the essence of \(x\) . what explains the existence of \(x\) ? if it were its essence, then \(a\) , \(b\) , and existence together would explain the existence of \(x\) . but then existence would no longer be a part of its essence; it would be the essence itself, contradicting our starting thesis that existence is a part of its essence. could existence, as one part of the essence, explain the existence of \(x\) ? no, because then the existence of \(x\) would depend only on one of its essential attributes. then \(a\) and \(b\) would no longer be essential to \(x\) , and \(x\) would no longer be \(x\) . we therefore have things in which there is a distinction between essence and existence. these things cannot exist from themselves, since existence cannot be part of their essence. therefore they must exist because of something else. this chain is a hierarchical chain that needs a first member. in order to be the first member, there can be no distinction in it between its essence and its existence. the answer to the question what it is is therefore that it is. it is being or existence itself. st. thomas calls this ipsum esse subsistens , the subsisting act of being itself. since there is no distinction between its essence and existence, it is wrong to say that it is a thing in the ordinary sense. it is simply the act of being. summary of the first stage of the argument we can summarize the argument so far as follows: there are things in which there is a distinction between their existence and their essence. a thing can have an attribute either from itself or from something else. everything in which there is a distinction between its existence and its essence cannot have existence from itself. existence is an attribute. therefore, things in which there is a distinction between their existence and their essence have their existence from another. the chain of things that have their existence from something else must have a first member. in the first member of a chain of things that have their existence from something else, there can be no distinction between its existence and its essence. therefore, there is something in which there is no distinction between its existence and its essence. second stage of the argument we have shown that there must be at least one thing whose essence is existence. now we must show that such a thing can plausibly be called “god.” to do this, we need to recall the previous argument. aristotle argued that whatever is in potency to a property needs something actual to actualize that potency. we criticized the argument because it does not lead to a terminus of all chains of potency-actualization, but only to the claim that each chain has a terminus, not necessarily that there is one terminus for all chains. we also noted that feser, probably because he is aware of this fallacy, defends another version of the argument that is very similar to this argument. in his argument, he does not reason from all potencies being actualized, but specifically from the chain of the potential to exist. take the following chain as an example. the potential of iced tea to be warmed is actualized by room temperature. room temperature’s potential for heat is actualized by the fire in the tiled stove. here the chain of the potential to be warmed ends, because fire is essentially hot. there can be no cold fire; it has neither the potential for cold nor for heat. but fire has other potencies, namely the potential to exist. just as the heat-chain must end in something that has no potency for heat that needs to be actualized, the existence-chain ends in something that has no potential for existence because it is essentially existent. here the connection to the de ente argument becomes obvious. i prefer this variant because “potential to exist” is very unintuitive, since we are speaking of the potential to exist at every moment, not only when something begins to exist. the formulation in terms of “participation in existence” is, in my opinion, much clearer and more intuitive. but feser makes another mistake in the second stage of his aristotelian argument. without giving an additional argument, he moves from an unmoved mover that has actual existence without having potential for existence, to an unmovable mover that has no potency at all, that is, something that is pure act, what st. thomas calls actus purus . he does later give an argument in answer to a possible objection in the chapter “why an unmovable mover,” but there he addresses only that the unmoved mover cannot have potential for a substantial property; he does not address whether an unmoved mover could have potential for accidents. the divine attributes he ascribes to the unmoved mover are derived from an unmovable mover, that is, from something that has no potency but is pure act. in his thomistic argument, he also does not derive all the attributes directly from ipsum esse subsistens , but gives a small argument for why ipsum esse subsistens must also be actus purus and then derives the divine attributes from that. but his argument that ipsum esse subsistens must also be actus purus is also defective and establishes only that ipsum esse subsistens must be pure act with respect to existence . that is simply what ipsum esse subsistens already is if we use the act-potency formulation rather than the participation formulation of this argument. this objection was raised by joe schmid. feser addresses the criticism in a blog post [feser 2021], but in my judgment he dismisses it more than he gives a real counterargument. tyler mcnabb also responded to schmid’s objections [mcnabb 2024], but joe schmid has answered that criticism as well [schmid 2024-3]. rob koons, however, develops in three blog posts [koons 2021-1; koons 2021-2; koons 2024] a completely independent argument for why ipsum esse subsistens must also be pure act. we will now defend that argument and then show why actus purus must be god. but first we must explain the thomistic technical terms substance and accident . to avoid complete confusion, we will give a brief overview of the thomistic terms already used, such as essence and existence, matter and form, and act and potency, and how they relate to one another. substance, accident, and further thomistic terms we mentioned earlier that a material substance is composed of form and matter, where form and matter relate to one another as act and potency. more precisely, a substance is composed of existence and essence, which in turn relate to one another as act and potency. the essence is what is, more precisely, composed of form and matter. by transitivity of properties, however,
