accident helps us see the meaning: accidentally means contingently or non-essentially. accidents are therefore the non-essential properties of a thing. by accidental we do not mean “without explanation,” but “not necessary for the thing .” brown-hairedness, for example, is an accident, because a brown-haired human being would still be human even if he changed his hair color. this differs from animality, because a human being who is not also a certain kind of animal is not a human being. here we are not distinguishing between separable and inseparable accidents. a complete example with a human being: my body is the matter that, through my soul as form , constitutes my essence. that i exist is due to god’s causing my essence to participate in the existence of ipsum esse subsistens . when my essence exists, it is a substance . it then has within itself everything necessary to exist. but to describe me completely, one must also know my accidental properties, my accidents . these do not have per se existence; they do not possess existence in the way a substance does. a substance can be sufficiently described in itself, while accidents can be described only in relation to the substance to which they belong. for what is brown-hairedness by itself? from ipsum esse subsistens to actus purus what we want to show here is that ipsum esse subsistens has no passive potency. that means it cannot undergo any intrinsic change. if there could be change in ipsum esse subsistens , it would have to be a change in accidental properties, since we have already seen that its essence is absolutely simple, because it is pure existence. koons’ argument that there can be no potency in ipsum esse subsistens is therefore that ipsum esse subsistens can have no accidents. first koons introduces the concept of a logical moment. a logical moment \(m_0\) differs from a logical moment \(m_1\) in that a cause exists in \(m_0\) , while its effect exists in \(m_1\) . this means that a cause and its effect can never exist in the same logical moment. the relation of logical moments that are before and after is, like the relation between temporal moments, transitive and asymmetric. two logical moments can occur in two temporal moments, but they can also occur in the same temporal moment. if a car participates in the existence of its parts, then the parts cause the existence of the car in logical moment \(m_1\) , while the parts exist in logical moment \(m_0\) , even if the causation of the effect occurs at a single temporal instant \(t_0\) . the next relevant principle koons introduces is the full complement of intrinsic properties . this principle says that if \(x\) can possibly have property \(p\) at some logical moment \(n\) , then \(x\) necessarily has either \(p\) or non- \(p\) at every logical moment \(m\) . the rationale is this: if \(x\) can have \(p\) , then it must necessarily have either \(p\) or non- \(p\) . one might ask whether \(x\) should not have \(p\) or non- \(p\) as a property regardless of whether it can possibly have \(p\) . after all, everything can only be brown-haired or not brown-haired. why should the fact that something is brown-haired at one logical moment in one possible world matter? the principle is meant to prevent us from multiplying properties beyond what is necessary. we do not want to say that “not having an interior angle sum of \(180^\circ\) ” is an actual property of a human being. since a human being at no logical moment and in no possible world has an interior angle sum of \(180^\circ\) , “not having an interior angle sum of \(180^\circ\) ” is not a property of a human being either, and of course neither is “having an interior angle sum of \(180^\circ\) .” the motivation for the full complement of intrinsic properties is that if \(x\) can have \(p\) but does not have it, this is not a mere absence , but a privation . if \(x\) cannot have \(p\) at all, then not having \(p\) is simply an absence; but if \(x\) could have \(p\) , then not having it is a privation. a smoke detector without batteries has a privation. a human being without an interior angle sum has an absence. privations are properties, because a thing is not completely described without reference to the privation. one can know everything about a human being without mentioning that he has no interior angle sum. but a smoke detector is not completely described if one omits the fact that it has no batteries. the last principle is this: both the ultimate explanation of a property and the ultimate explanation of its negation are ultimately positive facts. that a positive property \(p\) is ultimately grounded in a positive fact is uncontroversial, though koons gives additional arguments for it. if \(x\) is brown-haired, that is obviously grounded in a positive fact, namely his hair color. if \(x\) is only possibly brown-haired and not actually brown-haired, then according to the full complement of intrinsic properties , “non-brown-hairedness” is a property of \(x\) . this seems to be a negative fact, a merely denying fact. ultimately, however, it is positive. if \(x\) is actually blond, then this is a positive fact that ultimately grounds why \(x\) has non-brown-hairedness as a property. even if there is no such property, non- \(p\) would still ultimately be grounded by a so-called totality fact [cf. pickavance koons 2017: pp. 36 ff.], namely by the fact that there is a set of brown-haired things and \(x\) at \(m\) is not part of that set. this totality fact is itself a positive fact. positive facts, however, have causes. ipsum esse subsistens exists at the first logical moment, in which nothing exists except the essence that is identical with existence. at most, therefore, the essence of ipsum esse subsistens could be the cause of \(p\) . but then \(p\) would be an essential property, which we have already excluded. it therefore cannot be an accident either. consequently, ipsum esse subsistens can have no potency. ipsum esse subsistens is actual existence and has no potencies; it is pure act, actus purus . the existential inertia objection schmid and linford focus in their book above all on existential inertia as an alternative to the aristotelian argument or thomas’ first way. the objection would also apply in principle to the de ente argument, but here it is much less intuitive because of the participation formulation than it is in the cause-effect or potency-actualization formulation. the existential inertia hypothesis says that the existence of \(x\) at \(t_0\) is fully explained by the existence of \(x\) at \(t_{-1}\) and the absence of destructive factors. if we use the formulation that the existence of \(x\) at \(t_0\) must be caused by the actualization of a potential, existential inertia does indeed seem more intuitive. \(x\) exists at \(t_{-1}\) , so it would seem to have only a potential not to exist. as long as this potential is not actualized by something else, it should simply continue to exist. but if we analyze existence as participation in the existence of parts, then existential inertia cannot explain this. how could \(x\) participate in existence at an earlier moment if that moment no longer exists? take the following example: i destroy the backrest of a chair. under our participation analysis of existence, the chair exists at \(t_0\) and no longer exists at \(t_1\) . why no longer at \(t_1\) ? because its existence depends on participation in the existence of all its parts. under existential inertia , we would be committed to interpreting the destruction of the backrest of a chair as the destruction of the chair, even if my intention was simply to make a stool. the existential inertia hypothesis works only if we reject that an object has existence only through participation in the existence of its parts. derivation of the divine attributes 1st and 2nd divine attributes: uniqueness and simplicity something in which essence and existence are identical is absolutely simple, in the sense that it has no parts, neither physical nor metaphysical. in principle there can be only one such thing, because essences are precisely the principle by which individual, distinguishable things can exist. if there were two things that were pure being, there would be no principle by which they could be distinguished. 3rd divine attribute: being creator although this argument does not give us a reason to assume an act of creation in a finite past, it is still correct to speak of ipsum esse subsistens as creator, because everything besides itself receives its being only from this being. if, through independent arguments, we can infer a beginning of time, then ipsum esse subsistens must also be the cause of that first moment, since that first moment exists and is not ipsum esse subsistens itself. the argument even gives us a more necessary god than the kalam, because it shows that god is necessary at every moment in order to preserve all beings in existence. 4th divine attribute: eternity we have seen that ipsum esse subsistens has no potency. therefore it is also unchangeable. since time is a measure of change, ipsum esse subsistens must be outside time, and therefore eternal. 5th divine attribute: omnipotence for something to exist, the potential for its existence must exist. we have seen that this potential can be actualized only by ipsum esse subsistens . therefore everything that exists and everything that could possibly exist is caused by ipsum esse subsistens . it can therefore create everything possible. thus it is omnipotent. 6th divine attribute: perfection everything imperfect is imperfect insofar as it cannot fulfill its full potential. a cup has the potential to hold liquid. we can describe a cup as defective or imperfect if it does not actualize the potential to hold liquid. but in ipsum esse subsistens there is no potential. it can therefore have no defect. therefore it must be perfect. 7th divine attribute: goodness closely connected to perfection is goodness. feser argues that a thing is generally good insofar as it realizes the potentials proper to the kind of thing it is, and bad insofar as it fails to realize them. a good painter is good insofar as he has actualized the relevant powers of painting; a bad painter lacks them. but a purely actual cause of the world, free from potentiality, cannot be bad or defective. it must instead be perfect and, in that sense, wholly good [feser 2017]. 8th divine attribute: omniscience intelligence, as traditionally understood, includes three basic abilities. first, there is the ability to grasp abstract concepts, such as the concept human being , which does not describe only individual human beings or groups of human beings, but what it universally means to be human. this concept includes all possible human beings, not only those that exist or have existed, but also all those that could exist. second, there is the ability to combine these ideas into complete thoughts, as when one combines the concept human being and the concept mortal in the thought that all human beings are mortal. third, there is the ability to infer one thought from others, as when one concludes from the premises that all human beings are mortal and socrates is a human being that socrates is mortal. the ability to grasp abstract or universal concepts is the most basic of these three abilities. without such concepts, one could not form complete thoughts or infer one thought from another. to have such concepts means to have in the mind a kind of form or pattern that also exists in the things about which one thinks. there is a form or pattern that all human beings have, which makes them human. when these forms or patterns exist in material things, the various individual objects we find in the world result. but when we think about human beings or triangles in general, we abstract from the various individual human beings and triangles and focus on what they have in common. this is the essence of purely intellectual activity: the ability to possess the universal or abstract form or pattern of a thing without being that thing oneself. but for ipsum esse subsistens to be the cause of different things, it must individuate the actualization of existence in a determinate way. this means that it must in some way have an understanding of universals. insofar as it must have a kind of understanding of all possible universals and must itself be the cause of the particular existence of those universals, we can also call ipsum esse subsistens omniscient. we therefore have an argument for an absolutely simple, eternal, omnipotent, perfect, good, and omniscient creator. this we call god. we must note here that these attributes do not introduce complexity into god. it is not as if there were one thing in god that is eternity and another thing in god that is omnipotence . god is ultimately simple, without complexity. all the attributes of god ultimately describe the same absolutely simple essence, only in relation to different things and concepts. an analogy is light shining on different things. the light is always the same, but depending on what is held before it, only one color is reflected. the importance of this conceptual analysis we have now learned a great deal about the nature of god through this argument. this is very important. st. thomas did not merely derive the existence of god through this argument and then, once that existence had been proven, proceed with purely biblical theology. what thomas learned about god’s nature through deriving god’s existence shaped his entire subsequent philosophy and theology of god. the understanding that god is ultimately simple, without any distinction of properties, and that he is pure being itself, is important for understanding god. it informs the rest of the summa theologiae , the standard work that has influenced christian, and especially catholic, theology like no other work for centuries down to the present. st. thomas also connects this philosophical god with the biblical god . when moses asks god for his name at the burning bush [exodus 3:13], god answers: ego sum qui sum . this does not mean that god is a bee. in german, roughly: ich bin der, der ist ; in english, i am who am . thomas interprets this as biblical support for his derivation that god is being itself. jesus himself also refers to this old testament passage when he answers the jews [john 8:58]: original: amen, amen, ich sage euch: noch ehe abraham wurde, bin ich. translation: amen, amen, i say to you: before abraham came to be, i am. relation to the kalam recall that, in the conceptual analysis of the first cause of the kalam argument, we concluded that this cause must be outside time. what does that mean after we have introduced the thomistic metaphysical terms? at the very least, it means that none of the first cause’s potentials is being actualized, because otherwise it would change and would therefore be temporal. koons goes one step further. he says that eternity includes immutability. if a thing can in principle be changed, but is not changed, then it is not really outside time, but simply in a state of rest. so the kalam too shows that the first cause must be actus purus . thus from the kalam as well we can derive all the divine attributes we derived here. the two arguments for god therefore fit together very well and inform one another. leibniz’s cosmological argument the de ente argument can already be classified as a contingency argument: a subclass of cosmological arguments that infer a necessary cause because certain things have only dependent, that is, contingent existence, and do not have existence from themselves. one of the best-known arguments of this class is leibniz’s cosmological argument, which we will now examine. excursus: gottfried wilhelm leibniz gottfried wilhelm leibniz gottfried wilhelm leibniz (1646-1716) is considered one of the greatest thinkers of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries and is often regarded as the last universal genius . besides his important contributions to philosophy, he was also an important figure in physics and mathematics. in 1665 he won the university of leipzig’s honorary prize for the most beautiful wig. leibniz was born on july 1, 1646, in leipzig, where he began studying in 1661. in 1672 he received the opportunity to go to paris for four years on a diplomatic mission, at that time the capital of intellectual life. he spent most of the rest of his life in hanover, where he worked for the house of hanover. he died there on november 14, 1716. in philosophy he attempted to harmonize ancient philosophy and scholasticism with the modern philosophy of his own time. the principle of sufficient reason is one of his important contributions to philosophy. in mathematics his greatest contribution is the invention of infinitesimal calculus. he developed it in parallel with isaac newton. the last years of his life were spent in a bitter dispute with newton over who had discovered it first [stanfordencyclopedia 8]. the argument does not deal with chains of causes and effects. it is motivated by the total question: why does anything exist at all rather than nothing? here we will deal specifically with william lane craig’s version of the argument [craig 2010: p. 50; craig 2008: p. 106]. inspired by craig, we formulate the syllogism as follows: everything that exists has an explanation for its existence, either in its own necessity or in an external cause. the universe is a thing that exists. therefore, the universe has an explanation for its existence, either in its own necessity or in an external cause. (from 1 and 2) the universe does not exist necessarily. therefore, the universe has an external cause of its existence. (from 3 and 4) if the universe has an external cause of its existence, then god is the external cause of the existence of the universe. god exists. (from 5 and 6) here premises 1 and 4 must be defended. premise 2 is undeniable. premises 3, 5, and 7 follow from the premises. premise 6 must also be defended, but it belongs to the second stage of the argument. premise 4: the universe does not exist necessarily everything we observe in the universe is not necessary. everything we see can, in principle, be destroyed. what we directly perceive are almost always composite objects, things that have parts. whatever has parts cannot be necessary, since it is contingent with respect to its parts. could the fundamental particles of our universe be necessary? according to current science, at least, even fundamental particles can be destroyed. their energy remains conserved, but the particles themselves do not exist necessarily. is energy the necessary existent? energy is not a thing in itself. energy is a measure. energy can be transformed. take, for example, potential energy in the form of a mass above the ground. what exactly is its potential energy? not how large is it, but what is it? it is only a spatial relation between two substances. energy can also be converted into matter, so it does not exist necessarily as energy either. could the collection of contingent things be necessary? no collection of contingent things can be necessary, because as a collection it cannot exist without its elements. if even one element of a collection is not necessary, then the collection itself cannot be necessary. we therefore have good reason to believe that the universe does not exist necessarily. therefore it has an external cause of its existence. premise 1: everything that exists has an explanation for its existence, either in its necessity or in an external cause the first premise is in one respect a stronger claim than the first premise of the kalam, namely that everything that begins to exist has a cause of its existence, because here we do not restrict ourselves to what begins to exist, but refer to everything that exists. it is also a more modest premise, however, because we do not posit a cause, but only an explanation. causes are a subset of explanations. the first premise rests on the principle of sufficient reason , or psr. more precisely, it rests on a more modest version of the psr. leibniz formulates the stronger principle as follows [leibniz 1: 31-32, cited in pruss 2006: pp. 28-29]: original: kein fakt kann real sein, kein aussage wahr, ohne dass es einen zureichenden grund dafur gibt. translation: no fact can be real, and no proposition true, without there being a sufficient reason for it. why should we regard this principle as true? the first reason is that we always assume it in everyday life. we do not assume of anything we see or of any event we observe that it exists simply without explanation or happens simply without cause. the second reason is that the scientific method also presupposes the psr. scientists always seek causes and explanations for phenomena. no scientist would conclude that observation \(x\) has no explanation. the things science presupposes without explanation are exactly the things for which our psr does not require a causal explanation. these would include mathematical truths or logical rules. depending on one’s ontology, these are either not things that exist, or they are abstract objects that exist necessarily. our psr is also compatible with brute facts , that is, unexplained facts. craig illustrates the psr with an example from richard taylor [taylor 1991: pp. 100-101, cited in craig 2008: p. 107]. imagine that while walking in the forest you find a glowing ball on the ground. would you simply assume that it is there without any explanation? is there any property one would have to change in the story so that one would suddenly no longer expect an explanation? what could it be? certainly not color, shape, size, number, or complexity. this gives us good reason to accept the psr. stage two: if the universe has an external cause of its existence, then god is the external cause of the existence of the universe craig’s argument that the cause of the contingent universe must be god is basically this: the universe includes all spacetime. an external cause of the universe must therefore be external to space and time. we are therefore dealing with an immaterial and eternal cause. it must also be extremely powerful , since it is the cause of all contingent reality, and can therefore rightly be called creator . he further argues that we know of exactly two kinds of immaterial things: minds and abstract objects. since abstract objects cannot have causal influence, and since the cause of the universe is immaterial, it must be a kind of mind or intelligence . pruss gives further arguments for additional attributes [craig moreland 2009: pp. 90 ff.]. for the personality of the cause, pruss argues that we know three kinds of explanations of contingent things: scientific, personal, and conceptual. scientific explanations always explain circumstances through contingent things. every explanation of a substance through a cause is not an explanation through a concept. if the cause is therefore neither a scientific nor a conceptual explanation, it must be a personal explanation. the first cause is therefore personal . pruss also gives an argument for its simplicity . if a thing is composed, it makes sense in principle to ask why those parts are united. if the first cause had parts, then it would not be the ultimate explanation. relation to the other arguments perhaps it has become apparent that some hypothetical questions we asked here have already been treated in other arguments. to the question about the contingency of substances in the universe, we could have answered with the essence-existence distinction. to the question about the contingency of the universe as a whole, we could have answered with the beginning of the universe. in defending the psr, we could have reused arguments for the causal principle of the kalam. why did we not do so? first, because of the history and structure of the argument. leibniz and craig begin from very different assumptions than st. thomas, so they also use different arguments. while we tried to strengthen the first two arguments as much as possible, here we are presenting the argument more than fully defending it. second, it is advantageous when arguments are independent. this is true in a concrete probabilistic sense, but it also has advantages in dialogue with unbelievers. if an atheist rejects the basic assumptions of one argument, then he rejects only that one argument and not all the others, provided that the justification of the premises is independent. the moral argument the moral argument is also defended by william lane craig, although it is not one of the arguments on which he focused in his academic career. he is, however, co-editor of the blackwell companion to natural theology , in which mark d. linville gives a detailed academic defense of the argument. this is also not one of the arguments we want to defend fully here; we will mainly present it. for that reason we will rely especially on the popular version of the argument, inspired by craig, that the catholic apologist trent horn defends in debates and books. excursus: trent horn trent horn trent horn was born in california to a jewish father and a formerly catholic mother. after he became friends with a group of catholics at school, he researched the arguments for the catholic faith and eventually converted to catholicism in 2002 [everybodywiki 1]. horn earned master’s degrees in bioethics, philosophy, and theology. he is an apologist at the well-known american apostolate catholic answers . he is also a speaker, the author of many books, and hosts a successful podcast called the counsel of trent . horn has defended a broad range of catholic doctrines in debates, including the existence of god, the resurrection of jesus, the canonicity of the deuterocanonical books of the bible, and the catholic doctrine of justification. his main focus, however, is the defense of unborn life. horn formulates the argument as follows [horn 2013: pp. 104 ff.]: objective moral facts exist. these moral facts have either a natural or a supernatural explanation. a natural explanation is insufficient to explain moral facts. therefore, moral facts have a supernatural explanation. the second stage of the argument can be formulated as follows: if moral facts have a supernatural explanation, then god exists. therefore, god exists. this argument does not claim that one must believe in god in order to act morally. it does not even claim that one must believe in god in order to have knowledge of moral facts. after all, even paul writes about the unbelieving gentiles in romans 2:15: original: sie zeigen damit, dass ihnen die forderung des gesetzes ins herz geschrieben ist. translation: they show that the requirement of the law is written on their hearts. rather, the argument claims that if god does not exist, then there is no objective ground for the truth of objective moral facts. that means that statements about whether certain actions, and omissions of actions, are morally good or bad can be true only subjectively without god. according to craig, moral facts include both moral values and moral duties. premise 1: objective moral facts exist a first argument for this is that, even though there is disagreement about moral facts, there are at least some moral facts that practically every human being recognizes. every normal person agrees that it is evil to torture and kill an innocent child. most people would also agree that this is not a merely subjective fact. the second argument can perhaps ultimately be reduced to the first, but it takes the form of a reductio ad absurdum : if objective moral facts do not exist, then it is not objectively wrong to torture an innocent person for fun. it is objectively wrong to torture an innocent person for fun. therefore, objective moral facts exist. this version makes the dilemma clearer. it has the great advantage that only premise 2 can be attacked, and even that premise appears obviously true to almost everyone. the bad thing about this argument, and about the moral argument as a whole, is the following. many atheists understand that objective moral facts would require a theistic, or at least supernatural, explanation. for that reason they are willing to bite the bullet and deny the objectivity of moral facts. they may be thoroughly moral people, would never torture someone for fun, and feel disgust toward anyone who would do so. but in a debate, this formulation can make them unwilling to answer honestly. especially in a public debate, it sounds bad to say: it is not objectively wrong to torture an innocent person for fun . they therefore feel forced either to affirm a thesis they do not share or to evade the argument. the argument can thus degenerate into emotional manipulation rather than honest intellectual evaluation. premise 3: a natural explanation is insufficient to explain moral facts evolution can explain very well why most human beings have similar moral intuitions. human beings survive better in social groups. those with dispositions to kill and torture are more likely to be excluded from social groups and therefore have worse chances of survival. through evolution, after some time most human beings therefore share similar moral intuitions. but this cannot explain the objectivity of moral facts. if morality is the product of evolution, then morality does not show us what we should do, but what helps us survive. can my mind be the explanation of moral facts? no. as soon as we assume that there is more than one mind, my view of good and evil is no longer objective. can a society be the cause of objective facts? no. if it could, we could not say whether one society has better moral standards than another. can the golden rule explain morality? the categorical imperative, kant’s version of the golden rule, says: “act only according to that maxim whereby you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law.” other versions of the golden rule say: “do not do to others what you do not want them to do to you.” no, because such a rule presupposes deeper moral facts, such as: human beings are of equal worth . we have therefore excluded a series of promising candidates for a natural explanation of moral facts. the explanation is therefore probably supernatural. stage 2: if moral facts have a supernatural explanation, then god exists god already seems to be a good candidate for explaining moral facts. goodness is, after all, one of the classical attributes of god. the biblical god claims moral authority over others by demanding obedience to his commandments. through his transcendence, god would also stand above everything else, and his moral judgment would have a claim to superiority over the moral judgments of his creatures. there is, however, an alternative explanation: moral facts are platonic objects. perhaps this alternative explanation could also be classified as a natural explanation. excursus: plato plato plato (429?-347 bc) was a philosopher in ancient greece. he was born into an aristocratic family. plato was a student of socrates, who left no writings of his own. most of what is known about socrates comes from plato’s writings. after traveling widely in the region from greece to italy, plato founded his famous academy in 380 bc, the precursor of our modern universities. in this academy plato then became the teacher of aristotle. he died in athens in 348 bc [britannica 1]. plato is known especially for the socratic dialogues, his theory of forms, and his allegory of the cave. according to plato’s theory of forms, universals such as catness , stoneness , and the like, that is, what all cats or stones have in common, exist as abstract objects independently of the natural world. a cat is a cat not by an intrinsic property, as in aristotle, but because it stands in relation to the abstract object of catness . other examples of platonic objects are numbers as such. according to a theory of moral facts as platonic objects, an action is good or evil because it stands in a certain relation to an abstract object. horn does not adequately address this hypothesis in his book. craig addresses it somewhat better [craig 2008: pp. 178 ff.]. his best argument is that platonism cannot explain the morality of moral duties, which are part of moral facts. how, for example, could failing to help be evil? it is precisely the absence of an action. since an action has not been actualized, it cannot stand in relation to an abstract object. counterargument: the euthyphro dilemma craig summarizes the dilemma from one of plato’s dialogues as follows: either something is good because god wills it, in which case goodness seems arbitrary, or god wills something because it is good, in which case goodness seems independent of god. this dilemma does not take account of a third alternative. god simply is goodness itself and could not be otherwise. the dilemma is like saying: everything is either outside or inside; where is the house? the house is neither outside nor inside, because it is the standard by which outside and inside are measured. criticism of the argument if objective moral facts exist, then we really do have a good reason to believe that god exists. here we have excluded all the promising alternative explanations, though of course in principle there could be other explanations. the problem with the argument is that the case for premise 1 can easily degenerate into emotional manipulation rather than honest intellectual evaluation. the moral argument represents its own class of arguments for god. after four cosmological arguments, we now turn to the next class: teleological arguments. the term teleology has its roots in the greek telos , which means purpose or end. it describes the goal toward which a substance or an action is directed. st. thomas presents in his five ways a rather general teleological argument, in the sense that it sees in all substances an end toward which they are directed. since only intelligence can direct something toward an end, unintelligent substances must be directed toward their telos by something deeper. in what follows, however, we will look more closely at two arguments that were probably more influential: arguments from specific facts about the universe to the conclusion that it was ordered by an intelligence. paley’s watchmaker analogy paley’s watchmaker argument is the first teleological argument we will consider. it is the argument chiefly attacked by richard dawkins, the leader of the new atheists . excursus: william paley william paley william paley (1743-1805) was an english anglican priest, philosopher, and author. after his studies he was ordained a priest in 1767. later he taught at christ’s college and then became rector in various places. in 1782 he became archdeacon. he is known especially for his watchmaker analogy [britannica 2; wikipedia 2]. excursus: richard dawkins richard dawkins richard dawkins (born march 26, 1941) is a british biologist. from 1995 to 2008 dawkins was professor at the university of oxford. he became known as the author of the selfish gene , in which he analyzes evolution from the perspective of genes rather than from the perspective of the whole organism. the book is also the origin of the word meme , which he introduces in order to describe a mental concept by analogy with a gene. according to him, an abstract idea, a meme , can spread and mutate like a gene [wikipedia 3]. dawkins is known as one of the four horsemen of new atheism, along with christopher hitchens, sam harris, and daniel dennett. new atheism is an atheistic movement of the twenty-first century that defends a humanist and naturalist worldview [wikipedia 4]. its criticism focused especially on christian fundamentalism and the intelligent design movement. besides his appearances in debates and discussions on the topic, dawkins’ most important contributions to the movement are especially his books the blind watchmaker and the god delusion . william lane craig successfully debated all four horsemen. feser answered dawkins’ arguments in his book the last superstition . paley’s argument a shortened version of paley’s analogy runs like this [paley 1: pp. 9 ff.]. suppose i came across a stone on a heath and was asked how the stone got there. i might answer that it had always been there, and that answer would be difficult to refute. but if i found a watch on the ground and was asked how it got there, i would not say that it had always been there. why not? because the watch, unlike the stone, shows clear signs of design: its parts are arranged to fulfill a specific purpose, namely to tell time. such an arrangement points to a maker, someone who understood its construction and intended its purpose. according to paley, the conclusion from this hypothetical scenario would not change if i had never seen a watch or met a watchmaker. we can recognize an intelligent designer, for example, in ancient art or ancient machines, even if we do not know their function [see, for example, jimmyakin 2024]. nor would the conclusion change if some parts of the watch did not work or seemed to serve no purpose. we would also not regard it as more probable that the watch arose by pure chance. his point is this: when we look at the universe, we see many examples of complex structures that fulfill functions, especially in biology. therefore we should infer an intelligent designer here as well, namely god. criticism of the argument the main criticism of the argument is that we have examples of entirely natural processes that generate complexity without a designer behind them. the primary example, of course, is the theory of evolution, according to which complexity arises from three quite simple principles: there are self-replicators. the self-replicators make errors in their self-replication, that is, mutations. depending on their environment, self-replicators with different mutations have different probabilities of how often they can replicate themselves. the theory of evolution is accepted by the vast majority of scientists and is an example of a natural process that generates complexity without a designer. paley wrote his watchmaker analogy about sixty years before charles darwin published on the origin of species . another example of such a process is conway’s game of life . this is a kind of computer game, though after the player has set the initial conditions, he no longer intervenes and the game develops deterministically. it consists of a matrix of white dead cells and black living cells. at the beginning, the player determines which cells are black or white. after that, the game follows four simple rules: any live cell with fewer than two live neighbors dies, as if by underpopulation. any live cell with more than three live neighbors dies, as if by overpopulation. any live cell with two or three live neighbors remains alive until the next generation. any dead cell with exactly three live neighbors becomes alive. if only a few cells are configured correctly at the beginning, complex structures can be created, such as still lifes, oscillators, and figures that create new figures , and even self-replicators . we therefore have good reasons to believe that complexity is not necessarily a good indicator of design. the fine-tuning argument the fine-tuning argument is a kind of modern version of paley’s watchmaker analogy. but besides the fact that it focuses not on biological facts but on facts about the universe, it also takes a concrete logical form and is not merely an analogy. the argument basically concerns physical constants. these are values in our physical theories that are simply numbers with a constant value, not derived from any laws of nature or more fundamental physical principles. precisely because they have no more fundamental physical explanation, they could theoretically have taken many different values. but only a very small range of values is sufficient for a universe in which life can arise. in both formulations, the basic argument is that our universe, as it is, is much more probable if god exists than if he does not. natural constants physical constants are, as already indicated, fixed numerical values that appear in physical laws and have no deeper physical explanation. one example is newton’s law of gravitation: \[ f = g \cdot  rac{m_1 m_2}{r^2} \] here the gravitational force \(f\) does not result only from the masses \(m\) of two objects and their distance \(r\) , but also from \(g\) . but what is \(g\) ? \(g\) is simply a constant numerical value, namely \(6.67430\cdot10^{-11}m^3kg^{-1}s^{-2}\) [nist 1]. this value comes purely from empirical observations. fine-tuned constants are physical constants that could take a range of values, but only a small subset of those values allows a universe in which life can exist. examples of such constants are [barnes 2017]: cosmological constant the cosmological constant \(\lambda\) describes, in einstein’s equations of general relativity, a force that causes the expansion of the universe. the ratio of values that allow life in the universe to those that do not, \(r_{\lambda}\) , is \( rac{1}{10^{110}}\) . amplitude of primordial fluctuations there were fluctuations in the distribution of density in the early universe. the amplitude of these fluctuations is called the amplitude of primordial fluctuations , \(q\) [rees 1999: p. 114; tegmark rees 1998]. the ratio \(r_q\) is at most \(10^{-4}\) . gravitational coupling constant for long-lived stars to exist, the mass of a proton must be much smaller than the planck mass. this ratio, \[ \alpha_g =  rac{m_{	ext{proton}}^2}{m_{	ext{planck}}^2}, \] is the gravitational coupling constant . the ratio \(r_{\alpha_g}\) is at most \(10^{-33}\) . ratio of the quark masses the relevant range in the masses of the up and down quarks is also extremely small if life is to be possible. the ratio \(r_{	ext{quarks}}\) is at most \(10^{-42}\) . for all these constants \(k\) , \(r_k\) gives the ratio of the life-permitting range of values for \(k\) to the relevant total range of possible values \mid nsu \land k') \ll 1\) . given that we have good evidence of fine-tuning, lpu is not improbable under t : \(p(lpu \mid t \land k')

probability function. lpu stands for life-permitting universe . nsu is the rival to the hypothesis t and stands for naturalistic single-universe hypothesis . \(k'\) denotes the properly selected background facts, and \(\ll\) means much, much smaller . the background information \(k'\) consists precisely in the facts about fine-tuning, such as the necessary values for the cosmological constant or the ratio of the quark masses, which we introduced above. the restricted likelihood principle is a restricted version of the likelihood principle , which is itself simply an application of conditional probability to the comparison of hypotheses. it is also integral to the definition of the word evidence . according to the likelihood principle , evidence \(e\) supports hypothesis \(h_1\) over \(h_2\) if: \[ p(e \mid h_1) > p(e \mid h_2). \] the degree to which \(e\) supports \(h_1\) over \(h_2\) is: \[  rac{p(e \mid h_1)}{p(e \mid h_2)}. \] the restricted likelihood principle is the same, except that ad hoc hypotheses are excluded, that is, hypotheses with no independent motivation. this restriction is necessary because it excludes tailor-made hypotheses. suppose lottery numbers are drawn, and the numbers are 874379. i could then propose the hypothesis that there is a demon who likes manipulating lottery numbers and whose favorite number is 874379. this hypothesis would now make the drawn numbers much more probable than pure chance, if we did not exclude ad hoc hypotheses. the argument says, in short: we know about the fine-tuning of the universe. a life-permitting universe is very improbable under nsu given the relevant background information. a life-permitting universe is not very improbable under theism. therefore the fact that life is possible in the universe strongly supports the hypothesis that god exists over the hypothesis that there is only a single purely natural universe, nsu . as mentioned, the argument rests on conditional probabilities. to explain these, consider a small example. suppose a friend goes to a casino from 8 to 9 pm to play a dice game with the simple rule: roll sixty times; if every roll is a six, you win 1,000,000 euros. what should we assume about our friend’s possible win at 9 pm? without further information, we should rationally assess the probability that our friend won as follows. the number of successful outcomes is 1: every throw is a six. the number of possible outcomes is \(6^{60}\) . according to the so-called principle of indifference , we should estimate the probability of winning as the quotient of successful outcomes and possible outcomes: \[  rac{1}{6^{60}} \approx 2 \cdot 10^{-47}. \] if \(g\) stands for winning, we write \(p(g) \approx 2 \cdot 10^{-47}\) . this is the a priori probability, the probability without further knowledge of the circumstances. at 9 pm we learn that our friend did in fact win. but we know that our friend rigs dice as a hobby, and we also know that the dice in the casino are handed out by a good friend of his. we now formulate the independently motivated hypothesis \(b\) : cheating was involved. the alternative explanation \(z\) is pure chance. since chance gives no deeper explanation of the win, the probability of \(g\) under \(z\) is: \[ p(g \mid z) \approx 2 \cdot 10^{-47}, \] so \(p(g \mid z) \ll 1\) . but because of our background knowledge, we have good reasons to assume that: \[ p(g \mid b) 
ot\ll 1. \] we can therefore say that the fact of the win strongly supports the cheating hypothesis over the chance hypothesis. craig’s version william lane craig formulates the argument, in his usual deductive form, as follows: the fine-tuning of the universe is due either to physical necessity, chance, or design. the fine-tuning of the universe is not due to physical necessity or chance. therefore, it is due to design. collins’ version has the great advantage of avoiding part of the second stage of the argument. since the argument necessarily has to do with probabilities, it is more natural to formulate the whole argument probabilistically rather than deductively. therefore we will defend collins’ version here. many of the arguments for collins’ version can also be used for craig’s version. premise 1: given that we have good evidence of fine-tuning, lpu is very improbable under nsu collins must show that: \[ p(lpu \mid nsu \land k') \ll 1. \] his argument has two steps: by the definition of a fine-tuned constant, the probability for every fine-tuned constant \(c\) is \(p(c) =  rac{w_r}{w_r} \ll 1\) , where \(w_r\) is the life-permitting range for \(c\) and \(w_r\) is the range of all possible values. since nsu and \(k'\) give no reason why \(c\) should fall in \(w_r\) rather than elsewhere in \(w_r\) , \(p(lpu \mid nsu \land k') =  rac{w_r}{w_r}\) , so \(p(lpu \mid nsu \land k') \ll 1\) . nsu is the hypothesis that there is a single purely natural universe. under this hypothesis there is no deeper explanation for the fine-tuned constants. since lpu , a universe in which life is possible, depends on the values of the constants, and since these have no deeper explanation and could vary, the explanation for lpu under this hypothesis is pure chance. the probability that a single constant has the correct value is therefore, as already indicated, the ratio of the possible values of the constant to the values that allow life. fine-tuning requires several constants to have the right values. in principle, the probability of lpu under nsu and the given fine-tuning would be the probability of fine-tuning, that is, the probability that all the constants have the right values. this would basically be the product of the probabilities of the individual constants. in practice it is more complicated, because not all probabilities are stochastically independent. but there are still ways to calculate the probability of fine-tuning. all collins needs for his argument is that the probability is much smaller than 1, and that is certainly the case here. the probability of the cosmological constant alone is \( rac{1}{10^{110}}\) . for comparison: the number of seconds since the big bang is about \(10^{17}\) . premise 2: given that we have good evidence of fine-tuning, lpu is not improbable under t here we must show that it is not improbable that a universe in which life can exist would exist if we assume that god exists. at first i was very skeptical of the fine-tuning argument because of this premise. my thought was this: god could just as well have created all sorts of other universes, with all sorts of other values for the constants. so the probability of a life-permitting universe under the god hypothesis is just as low. but this rested on a false understanding of free will. even if god had the power to create all other universes, and even if a completely free will means that nothing can prevent him from doing so, it does not follow that the result of god’s free decision is simply probabilistic. god can still have reasons for his decision. what reasons might god have? if god is a perfect being, then we can imagine two good reasons, motivated by swinburne [swinburne 2004: pp. 99-106, cited in craig moreland 2009: p. 254]: goodness and aesthetics. the first paragraph of the catechism of the catholic church says, in part: original: gott ist in sich unendlich vollkommen und glucklich. translation: god, infinitely perfect and blessed in himself. the catechism then says that, in a plan of pure goodness, god freely created man so that he might share in god’s blessed life [ccc 1]. god’s motivation could be that creatures participate in his goodness and beauty, and in the goodness and beauty of his creation. since this motivation can be satisfied by human creatures, we have good reason to assume that god would create a life-permitting universe. since god is perfect by definition, he cannot have a self-directed motivation for creation. his only motivation can be directed toward creation itself. premise 3: t is independently motivated recall why t must be independently motivated. a hypothesis may not be introduced merely in order to explain the facts. this is certainly the case here. belief in god has many independent causes and was already present before we knew anything about fine-tuning. counterargument 1: the anthropic principle the anthropic principle says, in short: we should not be surprised by fine-tuning, because if there were no fine-tuning, we could not ask the question in the first place. our perception is biased, because an observer selection effect occurs, whereby the only observable universes are precisely those that are fine-tuned. the problem with this counterargument is that it is not really a counterargument at all. it attacks none of the premises. to show why the anthropic principle merely evades the problem, consider this example. imagine that we are standing before a firing squad of ten well-trained soldiers. we are blindfolded, hear ten shots, and are still alive. we can now formulate different hypotheses. did all the soldiers miss? was the firing squad shot by soldiers from another army? did the soldiers deliberately shoot past me out of pity? what we certainly would not think is: well, if i had been shot, i could not ask the question, so my perception is biased. no. the improbable event still demands an explanation. counterargument 2: the multiverse we have set up the naturalistic single-universe hypothesis as the rival to theism. but what if there are infinitely many universes with all possible values for the constants? then our universe would not be improbable. it would be necessary that we observe a fine-tuned universe. the first problem is that this is an objection to epistemic probabilities in general. it would be an objection to every hypothesis concerning improbable facts. all the stars in the sky could arrange themselves to spell out “god loves you, xy ; believe in jesus,” and this would still be no reason for xy to believe in god. we could have video evidence, dna evidence, and a murderer’s confession, and it would still not be evidence that the murderer committed the crime. another problem is that the multiverse hypothesis is often not independently motivated. many physicists defend the multiverse hypothesis today precisely because it explains fine-tuning. there are also physical problems with some specific multiverse theories, but we will not address those here. anselm’s ontological argument excursus: anselm of canterbury st. anselm of canterbury anselm of canterbury was born in 1033 in aosta, in what is now italy. in 1059 he entered a monastery in france. he later became prior there and subsequently archbishop of canterbury. today he is one of the 37 doctors of the church and is considered a central founding figure of scholasticism [stanfordencyclopedia 9]. anselm lived at a time when reason was applied to theology in an increasingly precise way. his motto was fides quaerens intellectum , faith seeking understanding. he therefore did not try to replace faith with reason, but to understand faith more deeply through reason. anselm’s formulation of the argument anselm gave several formulations of his argument. here we follow the formulation at the beginning of the second chapter of his proslogion [anselm 1: p. 117], which can be summarized as follows: god is the greatest or best conceivable being. a being is greater if it exists not only in the understanding, but also in reality. since god exists in our understanding and is the greatest conceivable being, he also exists in reality. criticism of anselm’s argument anselm’s argument, at least as formulated here, is not a successful or convincing proof of god. however, the argument has a reputation for being difficult to diagnose. none of the premises seems obviously implausible in itself, but once one reaches the conclusion, it seems that there must be either a fallacy or a hidden premise. the most successful criticism of the argument is probably the use of parodies. but even these do not show exactly where the error lies. rather, by reaching absurd conclusions, they show that there must be an error somewhere. the most famous parody comes from a monk named gaunilo. he argued that if one accepted anselm’s argument, one would also have to believe that a best possible island exists. after all, a best possible island that exists is better than a best possible island that exists only in the understanding. since this island is by definition the best possible island, it must therefore exist. the problem is that a best possible island is not a coherent concept and therefore cannot even exist in the understanding. could one not always imagine a better island with one more palm tree, a slightly longer beach, and one more beach bar? so the parody fails to show the precise error in the argument. it also fails as a parody, because there is a relevant difference between a best possible being and a best possible island. the philosopher josh rasmussen, however, identifies the fallacy of the argument [rasmussen 2015]. there is a difference between god and our concept of god, or our idea of god. anselm’s argument does not take this distinction into account. if we say that the concept of god exists in our understanding, then the argument would at most show that the concept of god must actually exist. but if the argument claims that god himself, as a being, exists in our understanding, then most people would reject that formulation of the premise, and the argument would additionally commit the fallacy of begging the question , since it already assumes its conclusion in one of its premises. plantinga’s modal ontological argument as already mentioned, st. anselm formulated several versions of the ontological argument. one of them defines god not as the best conceivable being, but as the best possible being. we remember that arguments about possible existence can be made with the help of modal logic and possible-worlds semantics. neither was part of the philosopher’s repertoire in anselm’s time. the philosopher alvin plantinga took up this version of st. anselm’s ontological argument and formulated it with this modern conception of possibility. excursus: alvin plantinga alvin plantinga the american philosopher alvin plantinga (born 1932) is considered one of the most important figures in analytic philosophy of religion and the most important representative of reformed epistemology. plantinga comes from an academically shaped immigrant family from the netherlands. he studied at the university of michigan and at yale university. in 1958 he received his doctorate in philosophy. plantinga’s work is marked by precise definitions and argumentation, especially in the discussion of the ontological argument for god’s existence and the question of the rationality of christian belief. he argues that belief in god can be rational and justified even without demonstrative proofs. his main work is the so-called warrant trilogy, consisting of warranted christian belief , warrant: the current debate , and warrant and proper function [viertbauer gasser 2019: p. 56]. dr. william lane craig called plantinga the philosopher who had the greatest influence on his thinking. plantinga’s formulation plantinga’s argument can be formulated as follows: if god exists, then he exists necessarily. necessary existence is an essential attribute of god. it is possible that god exists. therefore, god exists. as mentioned, the argument rests on modern modal logic. it can be represented formally as follows: \(g ightarrow  ox g\) \(\diamond g\) \(g\) that if god exists, he also exists necessarily is true by definition. it is also intuitively an essential attribute of god, should he exist. that god possibly exists also does not seem to be a controversial premise. what seems controversial is the inference. how can it follow from if god exists, then he exists necessarily and god possibly exists that god actually exists? this is a consequence of the so-called s5 axiom of modal logic. the s5 axiom axioms are the basic rules of a formal system, by which the theorems or propositions of that system can be derived. in mathematics, for example, if we want to prove an equation, we must show how it follows from axioms such as every number has exactly one successor . in formal logic, we must show which rules of inference are applied in order to move from premises to a conclusion. an axiom itself cannot be proven within its own formal system. the s5 axiom of modal logic says: \[ \diamond  ox x ightarrow  ox x \] so if something is possibly necessary, then it is actually necessary. this axiom is not especially exotic. it is also quite intuitive when formulated in possible-worlds semantics. if something is necessary, it exists in all possible worlds. if something is possible, it exists in at least one possible world. so if something is possibly necessary, that means there is at least one possible world in which it is true that it exists in all possible worlds. therefore it exists in all possible worlds. since our world is a possible world, it exists in our world as well. another point in favor of the s5 axiom is that it can be derived from the brouwer axiom in the s4 system. alexander pruss also gives further arguments for s5 [pruss rasmussen 2018: p. 18]. criticism of the argument the controversial part of the argument is therefore not the rule of inference, but premise 2: it is possible that god exists , more precisely, it is possible that a necessarily existing god exists . as we already saw in the kalam, it is not necessarily easier to show that something possibly exists than to show that it actually exists. what is fatal for the argument is its parody . unlike the island parody, this is not merely an argument intended to show the absurdity of the original argument, but an actual argument for atheism. from the s5 axiom it also follows that if god possibly does not exist, then god actually does not exist, given the premise that god, if he exists, exists necessarily. for if god, if he exists, exists in all possible worlds, and we find a possible world in which he does not exist, then he exists in no possible world. so just as possibly god exists necessarily entails that god exists, possibly god does not exist entails, under the same modal framework and divine-necessity premise, that god does not exist. godel’s modal ontological argument as we have seen, the most difficult premise of the modal ontological argument is that god possibly exists. kurt godel’s argument attempts precisely to justify this premise. excursus: kurt godel kurt godel with albert einstein kurt godel (1906-1978) was a mathematician and logician born in austria-hungary. because of his incompleteness theorems, among other things, he is considered perhaps the greatest logician who ever lived. godel received his doctorate in mathematics from the university of vienna in 1929. in 1931 he published his incompleteness theorem in the article “uber formal unentscheidbare satze der principia mathematica und einstein. after the outbreak of the second world war, he fled to the united states and, through einstein’s mediation, worked at the institute for advanced studies. in his later years he devoted argument as mentioned, the argument depends on five axioms. the definitions are true by definition, and the theorems follow logically. a1: either a property or its opposite is positive, but not both
