axioms, of which two can plausibly be attacked: that a property necessarily implied by a positive property is also positive, and that positive properties are necessarily positive. overview of further philosophical arguments we will now give a brief overview of further philosophical arguments for god. the remaining ways of st. thomas no overview of arguments for god can omit the famous five ways that thomas aquinas presents in the summa . st. thomas does not develop the ways very extensively in the summa . they are presented there as what he calls them: ways of finding god, and not more than that. in the way they are presented in the summa , they are deliberately not irrefutable demonstrations. the first way the first way is the argument from the unmoved mover, which we have already discussed. the second way the second way is similar to the first. here, however, the starting point is not the observation of act and potency, but the observation that there are causes and effects. since a thing cannot be its own cause, because it would otherwise have to exist before itself, it needs an external cause. we again arrive at a hierarchically ordered series, which in this case needs a first cause. this cause we call god. the third way this is his contingency argument, and therefore related to leibniz’s argument. thomas writes that if everything were contingent, that is, if everything could cease to exist, then at some point everything would have ceased to exist. since from nothing, nothing comes, nothing would exist now. but since something exists, not everything can be contingent. therefore something exists necessarily, and this we call god. especially controversial is his premise that if everything were contingent, then at some point everything would have ceased to exist. its justification is not obvious. some suspect that his argument is that, given infinite time, all possibilities would eventually occur. since everything could cease to exist if everything were contingent, that too would eventually occur. the fourth way the fourth way argues from so-called transcendental categories. classically, these are the good, the true, and the beautiful, though st. thomas divides the transcendentals somewhat differently. they differ from other properties because we see them in things by degrees and not merely in binary terms. but if we evaluate things by degrees as “more” or “less,” this presupposes a standard of the perfectly good, beautiful, and true by which we measure these things. this we call god. the fifth way this is his teleological argument, which we already briefly touched on. we observe regularity in the world, which indicates that not everything happens merely by chance, but that things are directed toward an end. unintelligent things, however, cannot set goals through intentionality. therefore the purpose toward which things are directed must be set by an external intelligent cause. this we call god. the argument from consciousness j. p. moreland formulates the argument as follows [craig moreland 2009: p. 296]: mental events are real, non-physical mental things that exist. specific mental and physical events are regularly correlated. there is an explanation for this correlation. a personal explanation , an explanation by an individual of a rational nature, differs from a natural scientific explanation. the explanation of the correlation is either personal or natural scientific. the explanation is not natural scientific. therefore, the explanation is personal. if the explanation is personal, then it is theistic. therefore, the explanation is theistic. the most controversial premise is that the explanation is not natural scientific. here one would probably have to exclude all natural scientific explanations and would still run the risk that there is a natural scientific explanation that no one has yet discovered. nomological arguments nomology is the doctrine of laws, from the greek nomos , “order established by man, law,” and logos , “speech, word, doctrine” [wiktionary 1]. these arguments say that a creative rational cause is the best explanation for laws of nature, because it avoids two extremes. humeanism, named after david hume, claims that there is no deeper explanation for how nature behaves. this cannot explain the regularity we observe. property-based theories, which claim that laws of nature are only generalizations of the powers of individual substances, are the other extreme. but these cannot explain all laws of nature, such as the conservation of energy. a creative rational cause of the laws of nature is a middle way that avoids the problems of both extremes [hildebrand metcalf 2021]. the argument from the applicability of mathematics there is a famous article by the physicist eugene wigner [wigner 1960] in which he wonders why a purely abstract concept like mathematics can be applied so successfully to the real world. william lane craig gives the example of peter higgs, who by studying mathematical equations at his desk predicted the existence of a fundamental particle that was only experimentally detected decades later, after enormous financial and technical effort [craig 2019-1]. if we posit an intelligent creator, we have a good explanation for why an abstract concept describes the natural world so well. craig formulates the argument as follows [craig 2019-2]: if god does not exist, the applicability of mathematics to the physical world is nothing more than a lucky coincidence. the applicability of mathematics to the physical world is more than a lucky coincidence. therefore, god exists. linguistic arguments baumgardner and lyon [baumgardner lyon 2015] argue that language plays an essential role not only in our subjective experience, but also in the material world around us: in human thought and communication, in the laws of nature, and in the specifications and functions of living organisms. as encoded meaning, language is ultimately not material. apart from something analogous to the human mind, there are no serious candidates for explaining how linguistic phenomena could arise. the reasonable explanation for the linguistic aspects of the laws of nature and of dna is therefore an intellect so comprehensive that most people would immediately identify this being as god. anthropological arguments anthropology, derived from the ancient greek anthropos , “human being,” and logos , “speech, word, doctrine,” is the study or science of man. peter kreeft formulates an anthropological argument from c. s. lewis as follows [cslewisinstitute 1]: every natural or innate desire in us points to a corresponding real object that can satisfy that desire. there exists in us a desire that nothing in time, nothing on earth, and no creature can satisfy. there exists something beyond time, earth, and creatures that can satisfy this desire. this we call god. pragmatic arguments pascal’s wager , named after blaise pascal, is a pragmatic argument. it says that we practically have a 2x2 matrix: god exists god does not exist believe in god infinite gain small loss do not believe infinite loss small gain we should therefore believe in god. if he does not exist, we suffer only a small loss, such as missing out on the pleasures of sinning. but if god exists, then we have an infinite gain in heaven. if we do not believe, we have an infinite loss, while in the case that god does not exist we have only a small gain. pascal, however, never conceived this as an argument for god. rather, he wanted to give the undecided an incentive simply to try living a christian life. the transcendental argument the transcendental argument, as defended by the eastern orthodox apologist and influential youtuber jay dyer, is a presuppositional argument . that is, it is an argument in which god is presupposed. the argument is a comparison of worldviews. dyer says that if we do not presuppose god, we could have no knowledge at all, because the possibility of knowledge presupposes certain things that can be explained only by god. he formulates it as follows: \(x\) is the necessary condition for \(y\) . \(y\) . therefore, \(x\) . here \(y\) is knowledge, and \(x\) consists of certain categories that, according to his definition, are transcendental and presuppose god. these include: space and time as such. the self. the fact that words have meaning, and that meaning can be communicated. the existence of the past. universals. ethics. all these things cannot be justified naturalistically or empirically, but they are prerequisites for our having knowledge at all [jaydyer 2022]. scientific arguments we have now received an overview of all the major philosophical arguments for god and will now take a brief look at scientific arguments for god, without going into any single one in full detail. scientific arguments do not follow a deductive form. in science, knowledge arises when theories are proposed that make predictions. if those predictions can be experimentally confirmed, this counts as evidence that the theory is correct. here we should notice a parallel with the fine-tuning argument, which could also have been classified as a scientific argument. there too we evaluated how expected certain observed facts are under different hypotheses. since a theory, that is, a hypothesis, implies its predictions and therefore expects them, a successful experimental demonstration of those predictions counts as evidence for the theory. but what if different theories make the same correct predictions? in that case there are criteria for selecting the best among the competing explanations. this kind of reasoning is called inference to the best explanation , and by analogy with deductive and inductive arguments it is also called abductive reasoning. excursus: abductive arguments in abductive reasoning there are certain facts, in this case scientifically established facts, and there are competing hypotheses that explain these facts. to select the best explanation, we evaluate them according to the so-called explanatory virtues . there is no universally accepted list of these, but mackonis [mackonis 2013] names the following: coherence : a hypothesis should not contradict our background knowledge. if we propose a hypothesis that explains our facts but also predicts that water flows uphill and snow is black, that counts against the hypothesis. breadth : an explanation is better the more facts it explains. electromagnetism as a fundamental force, for example, is a good hypothesis because it explains observations concerning both magnetism and electricity, which previously required separate models. here one also speaks of unification when a hypothesis explains not only many facts, but different kinds of facts. depth : an explanation can be deeper than an alternative explanation in two ways. first, it may describe a causal mechanism that produces the facts to be explained. second, the mechanism that produces the facts may be more specific, precise, illuminating, informative, or fundamental. the atomic composition of molecules explains their properties. subatomic particles, in turn, explain the properties of atoms. therefore subatomic particles are a deeper explanation of the properties of molecules than atoms, because they are more fundamental. simplicity : an explanation is better the fewer things and assumptions i must posit for it to work. lavoisier’s theory that combustion is a chemical reaction with oxygen, for example, was simpler than the phlogiston theory. the latter posited the substance “phlogiston” to explain why substances lost weight when burned. when it was discovered that some substances became heavier when burned, it had to be posited that some substances have negative mass, which made the theory much more complex. empirical adequacy : that the predictions of a theory are not refuted by observations is a necessary condition for a hypothesis to be a candidate at all. as mentioned, there are alternative ways of ordering the explanatory virtues . sometimes additional virtues are included; sometimes some are combined or divided. one criterion missing from this list is independent motivation . we already saw in the section on fine-tuning why a hypothesis may not be ad hoc . perhaps this criterion can be assigned to the virtue of simplicity, but that does not do justice to the importance of independent motivation. a scientific argument for god begins from scientific observations and posits god as an explanation for those observations. it then analyzes various alternative explanations and must show that the god hypothesis is the better explanation for the observed phenomena. this differs from using science within philosophical arguments. william lane craig, for example, also uses scientific arguments for his kalam. but there he does not present god as the explanation for the scientific facts. rather, he uses them only to support his premise that the universe began to exist, while preserving the deductive form of the argument. excursus: stephen c. meyer stephen c. meyer dr. stephen c. meyer received his doctorate in philosophy of science from the university of cambridge. a former geophysicist and college professor, he now directs the center for science and culture at the discovery institute in seattle. meyer completed his undergraduate studies in physics and earth science at whitworth college in spokane, washington, in 1981. he later became a geophysicist with atlantic richfield company (arco) in dallas, texas. from 1981 to 1985 he worked for arco in digital signal processing and seismic survey interpretation. in 1986 he began studying history and philosophy of science at the university of cambridge, earning a master’s degree in 1987 and a doctorate in 1991. his dissertation was titled “of clues and causes: a methodological interpretation of origin-of-life research.” meyer is one of the leading proponents of the intelligent design movement, which posits an intelligent designer as the cause of biological complexity and diversity. meyer has written two books on the subject, signature in the cell and darwin’s doubt . before publishing these books, meyer was especially known for a review essay published in august 2004 in the peer-reviewed biological journal proceedings of the biological society of washington . the article presented the case for intelligent design and presented it as the best explanation for the origin of the biological information needed to produce the new animal forms that appeared suddenly during the cambrian explosion. because the article was the first peer-reviewed publication arguing for intelligent design in a scientific journal, it proved extremely controversial [stephencmeyer 2024]. the geophysicist stephen c. meyer presents in his book return of the god hypothesis [meyer 2023] an actual abductive scientific argument for god. he does not explicitly appeal to the explanatory virtues , but presents abductive arguments in the following simplified form: if \(a\) were true, then \(c\) would be expected or unsurprising. the surprising fact \(c\) , considered in itself, is observed. therefore, \(a\) is probably true. here is an example of the schema: if the modern understanding of quantum physics is true, it is unsurprising that light has both particle and wave properties. surprisingly, it has been observed that light has both particle and wave properties. therefore, the modern understanding of quantum physics is probably true. in his book, meyer presents three scientific facts for which he posits god as the explanation: the beginning of the universe : here he argues especially from big bang theory. this theory was proposed by a belgian catholic priest and was initially rejected because of its obvious theistic implications. meyer also appeals to the borde-guth-vilenkin theorem , which shows that every universe that is on average expanding must be finite in the past direction. he also addresses competing cosmological theories and shows their problems. fine-tuning : his presentation of the facts about fine-tuning is similar to the facts we already presented in the philosophical fine-tuning argument. design in biology : here he does not argue, like paley, merely that complexity in general must have a designer. rather, he points out the problems of neo-darwinism. for example, the event known as the cambrian explosion is not what darwinism would lead us to expect. he also focuses especially on the complex information in dna and the difficulties of obtaining new complex functional genes through simple unguided mutation. for these three facts meyer presents god as the explanation. we can already see that the god hypothesis does very well with the virtue of breadth, since it can explain all three unrelated and diverse facts. it also does very well with respect to depth, since it explains the causal mechanism through the free decision of an omnipotent being. it is also relatively simple, because it posits only one further entity that is itself ultimately simple, namely god. elsewhere [meyer 2010], meyer even addresses the point of empirical adequacy. the intelligent design hypothesis in biology makes falsifiable predictions that turned out to be correct. one example is that the intelligent design hypothesis predicts hidden functionality in what at first appears to be “bad design.” critics of id , for example, cited pathogenic bacteria as an argument against the hypothesis. scott minnich, an id proponent, proposed that under his hypothesis the production of pathogens should be an effect of degenerative loss of original bacterial genes. he demonstrated this with the bacterium yersinia pseudotuberculosis . when he restored the gene responsible for producing the protein flagellin, he was able to show that the bacterium’s risk of causing gastrointestinal infection decreased [meyer 2010: p. 382]. naturalists might reject the god hypothesis under the heading of coherence, since we do not generally observe supernatural causes, and god as a supernatural cause would therefore contradict our background knowledge. this would be false, however, because we are not positing god as an observable supernatural cause. and with respect to unobservable supernatural causes, we have no contradictory background knowledge. the caution one should have with scientific arguments for god is the same caution one should have with science in general: science is always provisional. practically every scientific hypothesis that preceded those currently accepted has by now been superseded. almost all of the most brilliant scientists who ever lived were wrong, or only partially correct, about one, many, or even all of their hypotheses. if a scientific fact that we have explained by god is superseded, then that is not an argument against god. but that particular reason for god falls away, even if a new one may arise. this shows that a scientific argument for god can only be as good as the scientific facts on which it is based. arguments from miracles the catholic catechism defines a miracle as follows: original: ein wunder wird definiert als aussergewohnlicher sinnlicher effekt, der von gott gewirkt wird. translation: a miracle is defined as an extraordinary sensible effect worked by god. more fully, it is an effect that exceeds the power and order of created nature. the necessary features an event must have in order to count as a miracle are therefore: god alone as its cause. beyond the power of creatures. beyond the created order. extraordinary. perceptible. this definition corresponds to the intuition that a miracle must be an event that cannot be explained by the laws of nature and that must have a religious reference. the last two points, perceptibility and extraordinariness, point to the reason for miracles: god wants to give a sign that must unmistakably come from him. that is why miracles are good arguments for god: they are much better explained under the god hypothesis than under natural explanations. arguments from miracles basically work like scientific arguments. we observe surprising events and establish god as the best explanation. we can either argue, as in scientific arguments, by using the explanatory virtues for god as the best explanation, or we can use an approach with conditional probabilities, similar to the fine-tuning closely at the facts concerning some candidates for arguments from miracles, without undertaking a concrete evaluation. medical miracles: bruce van natta there are countless miraculous healings documented by medical reports. the subjectivity of illness often causes skeptics to doubt. in theory, pain, blindness, or paralysis can always be faked. but there are also at least two well-documented cases of healings of people with missing body parts. one of them is the case of bruce van natta. one evening, while van natta was working late, a jack gave way and the massive axle of a truck, weighing about \(22,000\) kilograms, crushed his abdomen almost to the concrete. blood shot into his throat, and he saw angels holding his body together. first responders considered him dead for about forty minutes, since because of his severed arteries he should have bled out within ten minutes. his survival was medically unexpected, and subsequent studies show that he is the only person ever to have survived such injuries. despite his survival, van natta’s abdominal injuries were severe. doctors removed most of his small intestine because it was dead or dying. he had only \(121\) centimeters of small intestine left, while the average length is about \(600\) centimeters. since he could not digest food, his condition steadily deteriorated and his weight fell from about \(90\) kilograms to about \(70\) kilograms. a friend flew in from new york because he suddenly felt the urge to pray for him. he commanded the small intestine to grow back in jesus’ name, and van natta felt an electric shock in his body and was healed. a radiologist confirmed that van natta’s small intestine had more than doubled in length and was now fully functional. van natta is still alive today and remains healthy. apart from this case, there is no documented case of a regrown intestine [keener 2021: pp. 127-128]. the miracle of the sun at fatima because of repeated apparitions of the holy mother of god to portuguese shepherd children, a great stir arose. since the seers were accused of lying, the seer lucia repeatedly asked the mother of god for a miracle. at the fifth apparition, the mother of god promised a miracle at her next apparition on october 13, 1917. in expectation of the miracle, many people made a pilgrimage to the place of the apparitions. after the vision was over, the sun began to dance in the sky and shine in colorful light [scharf 1984]. here are some facts established about the miracle: the miracle was observed by at least \(30,000\) to \(40,000\) people. it was observed by both believers and atheists. it was reported in local newspapers practically immediately afterwards. it was observed from many kilometers away. there was lasting physical evidence in that the clothing of many pilgrims, after hours of rain, was dry immediately after the miracle [dalleur 2021]. eucharistic miracles there are five miracles in which the host consecrated in a catholic mass also jesus after this brief overview of three miracles, we will now devote ourselves in detail to one miracle: the resurrection of jesus. this miracle is so central to the christian faith that st. paul writes in 1 corinthians 15:14: original: ist aber christus nicht auferweckt worden, dann ist eure verkundigung leer. translation: if christ has not been raised, then your preaching is empty. the entire christian faith depends on the resurrection. it is also an argument against every other religion and, of course, against atheism. there is an approach to the argument for the resurrection called the minimal facts approach . in it, only those facts are mentioned to which a majority of christian and non-christian experts agree. these are then additionally supported with arguments. finally, the miraculous raising of jesus from the dead by god is presented as the best explanation. this approach is defended especially by gary habermas and michael licona. william lane craig also uses a similar approach. here, however, we will argue more in the sense of a maximal data case after timothy and lydia mcgrew. our argument will have three steps. first, we will establish the credibility of our sources. then we will extract relevant facts from those sources. finally, we will defend a bodily resurrection as the best explanation of the facts. 1. the reliability of the sources first, then, we need to establish the reliability of our sources for the life of jesus. but what sources are available to us at all? we have the new testament as a source and two relevant non-christian extra-biblical sources. there are further extra-biblical sources, but they are either christian or their temporal proximity to the events is not established. more precisely, our sources are: the pauline epistles. the gospel according to mark. the gospel according to matthew. the gospel according to luke. the acts of the apostles. the gospel according to john. the annals of tacitus. jewish antiquities by josephus. the extra-biblical sources of josephus and tacitus mention jesus only briefly. tacitus reports that christ was executed under pontius pilate during the reign of tiberius, and that the christian movement then broke out again, first in judea and then in rome. in the writings of flavius josephus there are two mentions of jesus. one passage is highly disputed and is commonly interpreted as a later christian interpolation. in the less disputed passage, josephus reports that ananus assembled the sanhedrin and had james, “the brother of jesus who was called christ,” brought before it and stoned [mcdowell 1987: pp. 132-134]. these sources do not give us much information about the life of jesus, but they at least support the following facts: the actual existence of jesus as a historical person. the execution of jesus under pontius pilate. the existence of a movement that followed jesus. the death of james. should we rely only on these sources, since the biblical sources are biased? no. a non-christian source confirming the resurrection of jesus would be practically impossible. if an author really established the resurrection of jesus, he would himself believe in christ and become a christian, whereupon we would immediately exclude his source again. another reason is that most historical sources are simply biased. josephus, for example, writes in a very pro-jewish narrative. the solution is not to exclude such sources from the outset, but to take their bias into account when evaluating them. we will therefore now consider the reliability of the new testament sources as our sources. dating the roman historian a. n. sherwin-white establishes, using the example of the killing of the athenian tyrant hipparchus, that it takes more than two generations for myths to overlay the historical core of an event. it was a popular story that the murder of the tyrant hipparchus liberated the city of athens, even though the tyranny actually continued for four years after his death. although the myth was already popular about forty years after the murder, the historical core remained in the ancient historians herodotus and thucydides for at least two generations. for the historical core of the life of jesus to have fallen victim to myths, the relevant parts of the new testament would therefore have to have been written in the second century. but they were written much earlier. tacitus and josephus each wrote in the first century. there are several theories about the order in which the gospels were written. the most popular is the “q” hypothesis. according to this hypothesis, matthew and luke used mark as a source, since all three share many common narratives. mark is seen as the first gospel because it is the shortest, and later writings are generally longer, since the author tries, for example, to interpret and embellish the events according to his narrative. in addition, an undiscovered source “q” is postulated, because matthew and luke record many sayings of jesus that are missing from mark. the following diagram illustrates the theory: these three gospels are called the “synoptic gospels” because, as mentioned, they share much of their content. what is still missing from the diagram are the additional sources for luke and matthew, which explain the stories each records that the other does not. john is an independent gospel and is generally regarded as the one written latest. the latest possible dating for john is around the year 120, because the earliest surviving fragment, itself several copies removed from the original, comes from the first half of the second century [craig moreland 2009: p. 600]. according to the modern critical method, mark was written shortly after the year 70, because mark mentions jesus’ prophecy about the destruction of the temple. critics argue either that this is an insertion by mark in order to ascribe a prophecy to jesus, or at least that he would not mention it if he did not know whether the prophecy would actually come to pass. dating the gospels between 70 and 120 would mean that they were still written too early for myths to have erased the historical core. at that time many eyewitnesses would still have been alive, and there would have been an interest in refuting the stories in the gospels. by comparison, the earliest sources for the life of alexander the great are more than 300 years removed from his death. there are, however, very good reasons to date the gospels even earlier. first, there are problems with the argument from the destruction of the temple. if the argument is that mark would not mention the prophecy if he did not know whether it would come to pass, then why do the gospels mention jesus’ prophecies about his still future second coming, but supposedly hesitate to record prophecies about a not-yet-destroyed temple? if the argument is that this is an insertion by mark to ascribe a prophecy to jesus because prophecies are impossible, then that is simply an unjustified bias against the supernatural. luke never mentions the destruction of jerusalem in the year 70, even though he focuses strongly on events in the city. there are also positive reasons why the synoptic gospels were written before the year 70: in acts, luke tells in detail of his journey with paul and mentions that paul is awaiting trial in rome, but ends his account without mentioning the outcome of the trial. by mentioning paul’s condemnation to death in 64, he could have portrayed paul as a glorious martyr, yet he does not mention the outcome at all. the most probable explanation is that acts was completed shortly before. since acts is a sequel to the gospel of luke, which in turn was written after mark, the gospel of luke, the gospel of mark, and acts must have been written before 64. the attitude toward the romans in acts is positive. this is unlikely if it was written after nero’s persecution of christians in 64 [craig 2001: pp. 104-105]. matthew contains a passage in which jesus indicates that even though they are not strictly obliged to pay the temple tax, they should still do so in order not to cause offense. after the destruction of the temple, the temple tax continued to be collected, but now to finance a temple in honor of jupiter. if matthew had written at that time, he probably would not have recorded a saying of jesus supporting the payment of the temple tax [akin 2018-1]. matthew repeatedly relates the events he narrates to the present moment at which he writes. when he tells how judas returns the silver pieces and the jews buy a field with them, he adds that the field is called the field of blood “to this day” [matthew 27:8]. when matthew tells of the bribery of the guards at jesus’ tomb, who were to say that the disciples had stolen jesus, he writes that this rumor is spread among the jews “to this day” [matthew 28:15]. if matthew had written after the destruction of the temple, why does he make no reference to the fulfillment of the prophecy? [zahn 1909: p. 571] the gospel of luke and acts were therefore probably written before 64. depending on when paul’s imprisonment took place, they may even have been written around 60 [akin 2018-2]. the gospel of mark, as a source, would be even earlier. matthew, according to common opinion, was written between the two [habermas 2024: p. 782], so also around the year 60 and certainly before 70. the gospel of john is dated by majority opinion to the years 90 to 100 [habermas 2024: p. 832]. paul’s letters are dated even earlier. his first letter to the corinthians is dated around the year 55. in it, he quotes an early christian creed [1 corinthians 15:3-5] and mentions that he is handing on what he himself received: original: christus ist fur unsere sunden gestorben, gemass der schrift, und ist begraben worden. translation: christ died for our sins according to the scriptures, and was buried. he immediately then mentions the witnesses of the resurrection, and the only ones he names are peter and james. these are exactly the disciples he visited for fifteen days three years after his conversion [galatians 1:18-19]. it is therefore likely that he received this creed at that time, which means that it comes from the first five years after jesus’ crucifixion. nature of the sources after the very early dating, which because of living eyewitnesses leaves no room for the historical core to be dissolved by myth, the nature of the sources also points to their authenticity. the gospels are generally assigned to the genre of greco-roman biography [mcgrew 2019: p. 67], which means that they fundamentally aim to report historical events accurately. the authors also repeatedly appeal explicitly to eyewitness reports. luke begins his gospel by saying that many had already undertaken to write an account, that these accounts rested on those who were eyewitnesses from the beginning, and that he himself had investigated everything carefully [luke 1:1-4]. john likewise appeals to eyewitness testimony in the passion narrative [john 19:35] and again in connection with jesus’ appearances after the resurrection [john 21:24]. there is also a very old tradition that peter was the source for the gospel of mark. in his fourth-century church history , eusebius quotes the church father papias of hierapolis (c. 60-130), who says that mark, as peter’s interpreter, wrote accurately what he remembered from peter’s teaching, though not in exact order [eusebius 1: 3.39.15-16]. thus both the genre of the gospels and their appeal to eyewitness reports indicate that they did not claim to write a purely theological work, but to record historical events accurately. a counterargument would be that the gospels cannot be accurate historiography because they repeatedly contradict each other. examples would include smaller details of peter’s denial of jesus in the four gospels or the names of the women at jesus’ tomb. often, however, details mentioned in one gospel are simply not mentioned in another, which is not yet a contradiction [craig moreland 2009: pp. 597-598]. often alleged contradictions are simply the result of stylistic devices used in the genre of greco-roman biography. examples include addition for clarification, intensification, or explanation of certain points; omission for brevity; replacement by another term, usually a synonym; change in the inflection of a word, such as from singular to plural or vice versa; turning a speech or teaching into a dialogue; and changing a question into a statement or command, or vice versa [licona 2017: p. 197]. yet in greco-roman biography, despite all these stylistic devices, recording true facts stood above communicating one’s personal views, as we learn for example from lucian of samosata’s how to write history [mcgrew 2019: p. 103]. the important point is that none of this calls the factual historical core into question. for example, practically no authors agree about how many troops xerxes brought to his invasion of greece, but no one doubts the invasion itself [craig moreland 2009: p. 598]. the small differences are not only no argument against the accuracy of the gospels; they are even an argument for their independence. if an investigator hears exactly the same version of an event from two witnesses, this does not strengthen his trust in the accuracy of the reports, but diminishes it, because it is an indication that the witnesses coordinated their testimony. external support the next point in favor of the credibility of the gospels is that there is external support for the facts they record. we have already seen how tacitus and josephus support, among other things, the crucifixion of jesus, pontius pilate, and the existence of a jesus movement. another example is a passage in matthew [matthew 2:22], where joseph fears going to judea because archelaus is ruling there. matthew does not explain why joseph fears him. from josephus we learn that after some jews stoned a roman soldier, archelaus ordered the killing of \(3000\) jews [southwesternseminary 2017]. what the gospel presupposes for full understanding but does not mention can therefore be confirmed from an external source. external support also comes from archaeology. the french critic alfred loisy rejected john’s description of the pool of bethesda with five porticoes, arguing that it was merely a metaphor for the five books of moses. excavations in 1956, however, confirmed that the pool was located where john described it and that it really had five porticoes [craig moreland 2009: p. 600]. further archaeological support includes: the discovery in caesarea maritima in 1961 of an inscription bearing pilate’s name and title. the discovery of a boundary stone of emperor claudius containing the name sergius paulus, who is mentioned in acts as proconsul [acts 13:7]. the discovery of the pool of siloam, mentioned by john [john 9:7] [last three points: craig moreland 2009: p. 600]. the discovery of an inscription in antioch stating that quirinius was governor of syria at the time of the census, as luke writes [luke 2:2]. luke mentions “lysanias tetrarch of abilene” [luke 3:1]. the only lysanias ancient researchers knew had died before christ, until an inscription was discovered in damascus speaking of a “lysanias, ruler of the land,” dated to the right period [last two points: mcdowell 1987: pp. 123-124]. undesigned coincidences imagine that alice and bob met eve in a cafe. eve denies that the meeting took place. we now question alice and bob separately about the meeting. during the conversations, alice mentions in passing that the cafe was very crowded and that all three nearly failed to find seats together. bob mentions in passing that when eve turned around, she accidentally knocked over alice’s coffee and spilled it over bob’s trousers. these two facts fit together very well. the crowded cafe explains why eve spilled the coffee over bob when turning around: there was simply very little space. these two facts are also not a sign of collusion, since neither mentions the same fact as the other. the simplest explanation for such an undesigned coincidence is simply that both testimonies are based on the same event. the testimonies are coincidences because a crowded cafe and spilled coffee are unusual, though not necessarily improbable, events. they are undesigned because they mention different facts in passing. only when taken together do they give a fuller explanation of a circumstance. here are two examples of undesigned coincidences between the synoptic gospels and the gospel of john: in john’s gospel, jesus answers pilate’s question whether he is a king by saying that his kingdom is not of this world; if it were, his servants would fight so that he would not be handed over to the jews [john 18:36]. only a few verses earlier, however, john reports that peter cut off malchus’ ear with a sword [john 18:10]. how can jesus claim that his servants would not fight because his kingdom is not of this world if peter cut off the ear of a servant of the high priest? this makes sense only in light of luke’s gospel [luke 22:47-53], where it is explained that jesus healed malchus’ ear. without that independent fact it makes no sense why the jews would not bring malchus, with his missing ear, as a witness to pilate to show that jesus’ disciples really had fought against his arrest. if john were simply copying from earlier gospels, why would he leave out precisely the fact that, at first glance, resolves an inconsistency in his narrative? the simplest explanation is that he is not trying to fabricate a narrative, but simply recording the facts. before the feeding of the 5000, jesus asks philip where they should buy bread for the people to eat [john 6:5]. why does he ask philip specifically? philip is otherwise an insignificant apostle. earlier in john we learn that philip came from bethsaida [john 1:44]. only in luke do we learn that the feeding of the 5000 took place near bethsaida [luke 9:10]. we therefore have our explanation: jesus asks philip because philip comes from the area and knows it. here are two examples of undesigned coincidences between the synoptic gospels: in matthew’s gospel, matthew lists the twelve apostles in pairs [matthew 10:2-4]. when mark lists the twelve, he does not use this paired grouping. but later mark writes that jesus sent the twelve out two by two [mark 6:7]. mark therefore unintentionally explains why matthew lists the twelve in pairs. in matthew’s gospel, we learn that herod told his servants that jesus was john the baptist risen from the dead [matthew 14:2]. but how would matthew know what herod said to his servants, since he was not present? in luke we learn in a completely different context that joanna, the wife of chuza, a household manager of herod, supported jesus and the disciples [luke 8:1-3; mcgrew 2017: p. 88]. the disciples therefore knew the wife of a high-ranking court official of herod, which explains how matthew could know what herod said privately to his servants. finally, an undesigned coincidence between the pauline epistles and acts: in philippians, paul writes that he hopes in the lord jesus to send timothy to the philippians soon [philippians 2:19]. how did the philippians know who timothy was? at the beginning of acts 16, timothy is said to join paul on a journey [acts 16:1-3]. in acts 17 we learn that timothy remains behind in berea [acts 17:14]. although timothy is not mentioned in between, it is implied that he was with paul on the journey until berea. this shows that timothy was present on paul’s journey to philippi [acts 16:12]. this explains how timothy was known to the philippians. all these undesigned coincidences show that the individual works are all based on actual events. if they were invented stories, there would be no explanation for why the stories fit together so well. if the stories were copied, it would not explain why each author gives only one part of the event. one might argue that the later author invented the facts precisely so that they explain the other facts without mentioning them, in order to fabricate a more plausible forgery. first, this is an ad hoc hypothesis. second, it fails to explain why some facts between the works then appear at first glance to be contradictions that must be harmonized. for example, john [john 6:3-5] describes jesus seeing a large crowd coming from a mountain, while mark [mark 6:34] describes the same event as jesus the so-called minimal facts approach . this approach was shaped especially by gary habermas. it attempts to find with skeptics the smallest common denominator of historically establishable facts and then defend jesus’ resurrection as the best explanation of those facts. in the first part of his monumental work on the resurrection [habermas 2024: pp. 276 ff.], habermas lists the following as his minimal facts: jesus’ death on the cross. the experiences of the disciples. the earliest proclamation of the gospel. the transformation of the disciples. the conversion of james. the conversion of paul. william lane craig pursues a similar strategy, at least in his debates. he emphasizes that all his facts are accepted by the majority of new testament scholars. in his academic works he also goes beyond this approach. when he follows the minimal facts approach , he uses these facts: the discovery of the empty tomb. the appearances of jesus to the disciples after his death. the origin of the disciples’ belief. here, however, we want to focus on the approach of timothy and lydia mcgrew. in their article [craig moreland 2009: pp. 593 ff.], they presuppose jesus’ death and burial as established facts and make a bayesian argument from conditional probabilities based on three other facts. we will introduce these shortly. but first: how can we presuppose jesus’ death and burial as established facts? jesus’ death and burial the most important point is that we have many independent and early sources for them. his death and burial are first mentioned in 1 corinthians, where an early creed is quoted that was circulating in the early church only a few years, if not months, after jesus’ death. they are also mentioned in the gospels, acts, and the writings of the early church. tacitus mentions at least the death of jesus. paul, mark, and tacitus must at minimum be recognized as independent sources. we also know that paul and mark are very early, especially if we consider that mark probably uses an earlier passion narrative [habermas 2024: pp. 738-739]. bart ehrman lists more than twenty independent sources for the historical jesus, of which at least fifteen confirm the crucifixion of jesus, and he dates all of them within 100 years of the crucifixion [habermas 2024: p. 278]. jesus’ death is also an embarrassing fact that the authors admit, which speaks for its authenticity. the jewish understanding of the messiah was that of a glorious ruler, not someone who dies miserably on a cross. it is also unlikely that the burial story was invented, since the sanhedrin was naturally an enemy-image of early christianity. it is therefore unlikely that the authors would invent precisely a story in which joseph of arimathea, as a member of the sanhedrin, generously gives his tomb to jesus. w: the testimony of the women after presupposing jesus’ death and burial, the mcgrews’ argument rests on three sets of facts, which we will call \(w\) , \(d\) , and \(c\) . the first set, \(w\) , consists in the facts that jesus’ tomb was found empty by his female disciples and that he then appeared to these women. that the women found the empty tomb is described in all the gospels [mark 16; luke 24; john 20; matthew 28]. matthew describes jesus meeting the women [matthew 28:9-10], and john specifically describes his meeting with mary magdalene [john 20:11]. this is supported by the fact that it is very unlikely to be an invention, because the testimony of women had little value at that time. josephus, for example, writes that one should not admit the testimony of women because of the lightness and boldness of their sex. according to the talmud, if a man comes as the first witness, he counts as much as 100 women; if the woman comes first as a witness, she still counts as half as much as a man [craig moreland 2009: p. 608]. this is also supported by the fact that the disciples at first did not believe the women [luke 24:11]. the fact that the gospels give different lists of women is another point in favor, because these lists do not contradict one another, but nevertheless make direct copying unlikely. matthew also describes how the soldiers were bribed to say that the disciples had stolen jesus’ body [matthew 28:11-15]. this is probably matthew’s answer to rumors that the disciples really had stolen jesus’ body. but the circulation of such a rumor presupposes that the tomb was actually empty. if it had not been empty, it would have been much simpler to present jesus’ body than to spread such a rumor. d: the testimony of the disciples the gospels report the names of the disciples who claimed to have seen the risen jesus. they are the original twelve without judas. so we do not have anonymous reports; the eyewitnesses are clearly named. the disciples were also not predisposed to see a risen jesus. the jewish understanding was that there would be no resurrection of the dead before the end of the world. the disciples were also simply disappointed that jesus did not meet their expectations of the messiah. this is also clear from the story of the extremely skeptical thomas, who first had to touch jesus’ wounds before he actually believed. the experiences of the disciples were neither vague nor purely spiritual, but concrete, detailed, and empirical. how sure the disciples were is shown by the fact that they were willing to suffer and die for belief in what they claimed to have seen. they knew what had been done to jesus, and yet they continued to proclaim his message, caused disturbances themselves, were summoned before the sanhedrin, and were forbidden to continue preaching about jesus [acts 4]. shortly afterward they were also imprisoned for it [acts 5]. of some disciples we know with certainty that they died for the faith. james, the brother of john, seems to have been the first martyr among the disciples [acts 12]. we also know that james, the brother of the lord, was executed; josephus records this as well. he seems initially not to have been a follower of jesus. but paul specifically mentions jesus’ appearance to james, which explains his change of mind [1 corinthians 15:5]. peter’s martyrdom is also considered secure and is recorded by clement of rome. at the latest since the persecution of christians under nero and after these martyrdoms, all the disciples must have been aware of the danger they were in. one might object that islamist terrorists are also willing to die for their faith. that is true, and in their case too it shows that they firmly believe. the difference is that the disciples’ belief rested on first-hand experiences. why would they go to death for something, namely the resurrection, if they themselves knew that jesus had never appeared to them? c: the conversion of paul if the disciples were not predisposed to see a risen jesus, paul was even less so. paul was a fanatical persecutor of christians and had nothing to gain by changing his mind. his conversion also happened suddenly, which supports his testimony to the appearance of the lord to him. 3. explanation of the facts we now want to calculate, under the realities: atoms and the void. atoms are indivisible, infinitely numerous, different in size and shape, and have no internal gaps. they move in the void, repel one another, or connect by tiny hooks and barbs on their surfaces. apart from changes of place, they are unchanging, ungenerated, and indestructible. all changes in the visible world are caused by the movement of these atoms. macroscopic objects consist of clusters of atoms; changes such as growth result from rearrangements of these atoms. while the atoms are eternal, the objects composed from them are perishable. our world and the species existing in it arose through the collision of atoms and will dissolve over time. this, however, is not a modern theory. it is a summary of the teaching of democritus, a philosopher who lived before aristotle [stanfordencyclopedia 11]. naturalism is therefore by no means a more “up-to-date” theory than theism. “one god fewer” this too is not really a concrete argument. it can be formulated as follows: you christians do not believe in zeus, jupiter, wotan, vishnu, and all the thousands of other gods of other religions. we atheists do the same thing, except that we believe in one fewer god than you do. this argument would make a little sense if god were in the same category as zeus, jupiter, wotan, vishnu, and so on. but this is simply a false and simplified understanding of the christian god. god is not in the same category as these other “gods”; god is not in any category at all. as undifferentiated being itself, he is not even in the category of “beings.” he is radically other. that is also why practically none of the arguments for god lead to a being like zeus or jupiter. finally, we do not even necessarily believe that these “gods” do not exist at all. some of them may very well be demons. a stone so heavy this argument can be summarized as follows: can god create a stone so heavy that he himself cannot lift it? if he cannot create it, then he is obviously not omnipotent. but if he can create it, then there exists a stone god cannot lift, so he is also not omnipotent. or, as homer simpson put it [reddit 1]: could jesus microwave a burrito so hot that he himself could not eat it? the solution to the paradox follows from the fact that god’s omnipotence extends only to possible things. god cannot create a euclidean square circle. that does not fall under the definition of omnipotence, because a square circle is an incoherent concept. since for every weight a stone could have, god could lift that stone, a stone so heavy that god could not lift it is simply an incoherent concept. one can also approach the argument from the perspective of whether it is possible for god to limit his omnipotence. this is a debated question, but whatever the answer is, it does not reveal an inconsistency in god’s nature. one could also answer: “yes, god can create such a stone, but as long as he does not create it, he is still omnipotent.” divine hiddenness divine hiddenness is sometimes categorized as a subcategory of the problem of evil. it is an abductive argument and asks why god does not reveal himself more obviously. god could appear to every single human being and prove by means of a miracle that he really is god. why, then, does he not do this? first, we must acknowledge that, purely stochastically, this is a good argument. the number of possible worlds in which god does not reveal himself obviously is a subset of all possible worlds in which god exists, but it is congruent with the possible worlds in which god does not exist. put differently: if god does not exist, we would expect there to be no obvious revelations; if he does exist, we would expect obvious revelations. it is possible simply to accept this argument, but to say that the positive arguments for god outweigh this abductive argument. the other option is to doubt the premise that we should expect god to reveal himself in a completely obvious way. god wants us to love him freely. he gives us enough reasons to believe in him, but belief in god is not meant to be intellectual coercion. he always gives us a way out of believing in him; that is what makes it so valuable to love him freely. if a man believes that his wife loves him, he does not have 100% proof of it. she could still be a russian spy. but at a certain point one has enough good reasons to accept it, and then the man must trust his wife and leave the last 0.00001% doubt behind. and that is what faith means: not groundless conjecture, but trust . meager moral fruits the so-called meager moral fruits argument is partly popular on youtube and twitter. it takes the form of an abductive argument and can be summarized as follows: if christianity were true, we would expect it to bear moral fruit among its followers. that is, we would expect christians to act morally better than atheists, since they have closer access to god, the ultimate good. but we do not see this, which makes it less likely that christianity is true. however, we have no reason to believe that christians, and above all merely self-identified christians, must necessarily act better. christianity teaches that the consequences of the fall in the garden of eden are not eradicated even by baptism. the empirical part of the argument can also be doubted. if one looks at the lives of recognized saints, one sees unparalleled acts of charity and selflessness. the empirical premise also rests heavily on the fact that atheists often simply have a different moral sense than christians, especially on controversial topics such as homosexuality. but that atheists have the correct moral view here remains unargued. the problem of evil the problem of evil , or the problem of suffering , is the question of how an omnipotent and all-good god can allow suffering in the world. if he is all-good, he should want to reduce suffering; if he is omnipotent, he should be able to do so. why, then, do we see suffering in the world? thomas aquinas formulates it as follows [aquinas 2: part i, question 2, article 3]: es scheint, dass gott nicht existiert; denn wenn eines von zwei gegensatzen unendlich ware, wurde der andere vollstandig zerstort werden. aber das wort “gott” bedeutet, dass er unendliche gute ist. wenn gott also existierte, gabe es kein erkennbares ubel; aber es gibt ubel in der welt. daher existiert gott nicht. english translation: it seems that god does not exist; for if one of two contraries were infinite, the other would be completely destroyed. but the word “god” means that he is infinite goodness. therefore, if god existed, there would be no discoverable evil; but there is evil in the world. therefore god does not exist. the apparent contradiction is resolved by the fact that some goods partly presuppose bad things. heroism cannot exist without danger . mercy cannot exist without suffering . grace cannot exist without injustice . certain higher-order goods cannot exist without bad things. a more abductive version of the argument does not argue from incompatibility as such, but from the claim that the amount of suffering in the world is unlikely if god exists. the problem is that our assessment of what counts as too much evil is very relative. if the holocaust had never happened, what would the atheist then appeal to as the greatest and most improbable evil? also, we simply do not have the divine perspective that would allow us to judge when a suffering cannot bring about any counterbalancing good. the reason god permits suffering can be understood especially well through the devil. of course, the devil is a concrete person. but we can also understand him as the personification of evil itself. when, in goethe’s faust , the figure of mephistopheles , the devil, introduces himself, he says [goethe 1]: [ich bin] ein theil von jener kraft, die stets das bose will und stets das gute schafft. english translation: [i am] part of that power which always wills evil and always creates the good. this shows the eternal tragedy of the devil. he always creates evil, only to discover later that, against his will, it has brought about good. in the greek myth of sisyphus, sisyphus is condemned by the gods to roll a heavy stone up a mountain for all eternity. that means that whenever he has made progress, he sees that his path has not diminished at all. with the devil it is even more hopeless: he is practically rolling a heavy stone the whole time, only to discover that he has been rolling it in the wrong direction all along. bibliography akin 2018-1 -
