break with tradition. in effect, lg viii, by speaking of a real-ontological relationship between the church of christ and the catholic church, sets up the following dilemma: either “church” is used univocally - then subsistit , as a real relation, requires distinct entities, and there are therefore two churches, which contradicts tradition. or “church” is used equivocally - then lg implicitly imports a protestantizing separation of invisible and visible church, which would be even more foreign to tradition.[31] 4.3. justification of the contradiction after having presented some examples in which the fsspx contradicts the documents of v2, we must now clarify whether resistance to them is justified. after all, resistance to v2 is cited as the point preventing reconciliation with rome. first it should be noted that none of the controversial teachings in v2 was proclaimed as infallible. we have already discussed above that in this case public contradiction is justified under certain circumstances. this already follows from the fact that the church cannot in principle “force” anyone to accept a statement whose truth content is in principle knowable, when the church does not infallibly know that it is true.[32] but we have also discussed more precisely that the teaching of the church since v2 also allows this. we have further seen that the traditional guidelines in ott set far lower hurdles than the development since v2. but should the fsspx therefore make use of this possibility, or would it not be their task as good catholics to do everything possible to bring these statements somehow into harmony with tradition? the first problem is that, for example in lg viii, we saw how ratzinger tried everything to do precisely that, but we nevertheless ended up with an insurmountable dilemma. the fsspx recognizes by far the largest part of v2. in 90% of cases, v2 is completely in line with tradition, which in the current church crisis means that the fsspx de facto agrees with more of v2 than many of the heads of the church in regular offices. this statement can certainly be made with respect to the german bishops. nor does the fsspx know a black-and-white distinction between traditional teaching in v2 and modernist heresy. lefebvre himself spoke of a third category of texts that could be interpreted orthodoxly:[33] “there are some conciliar documents that are obviously in conformity with tradition [...] then there are some ambiguous texts, which nevertheless can somehow be “interpreted” correctly according to the previous magisterium. but there are also some texts that are plainly in contradiction with tradition and which can in no way be “integrated” with it” in lg viii we have already shown the clear dilemma and also shown the dangers to which such a formulation can lead. without referring to a particular text, we have also already shown, using the example of william lane craig, how v2 has worked outwardly and how this new understanding of ecumenism from v2 seriously endangers the salvation of people outside the church. does that not justify, or even require, a refusal to sign the texts? let us also recall once more what the situation was like in the arian crisis. there it was not even about individual texts, nor individual sentences, nor even individual words, but only about a single letter. at that time one could surely have interpreted “god-like” in an orthodox way even more easily than some conciliar texts: “god-like precisely does not mean that christ is not equal in essence to god the father. this formulation was used precisely to make clear that jesus is equal to the father in his divine nature, yet nevertheless differs with respect to his essence insofar as he has two natures.” a misunderstood hermeneutic of continuity would then have led even more people into false belief. in the arian controversy, as in selected conciliar texts, we see analogously how a text is false in its natural reading and how it is dangerous. even if we presume good intentions on the part of the authors, that is not sufficient. in the year 635, pope honorius, in a letter that today would be classified as ordinary magisterium, supported the heresy of monothelitism. honorius wrote:[34] original: “daher bekennen wir auch einen einzigen willen unseres herrn jesus christus [...]” translation: “therefore we also confess one single will of our lord jesus christ [...]” the interesting thing is that saint maximus, who fought against monothelitism, defended honorius. he argued that honorius had been misunderstood and had merely wanted to say that there were no contradictory wills in jesus.[35] he therefore interpreted good intentions into the heretical statement, but that in no way led maximus ever to sign such a statement himself. this is precisely the situation in which the fsspx finds itself. even if one can certainly accuse it at times of not always presuming the best intentions, this historical example shows how a good intention does not negate the statement of a text. whoever compulsively tries to interpret all v2 texts, which can indeed contain errors, orthodoxly places himself in extreme danger of falling into semantic relativism. this is a very great and little-discussed danger. 4.4. heresies from vatican ii lg 16 could also be counted among the non-harmonizable passages.[36] but i also want to show the danger of the harmonizable passages. it is not ecclesiastical practice to condemn only “non-harmonizable” statements. we have already seen how this was not the case with the arian formulas. the question that must always be asked is, “what does the text as such, in its context, intend to express?” from this perspective, statements that are not strictly heretical must also be condemned. to sign them would mean the sin of scandal, which we will address later in connection with the mass. the aim of this paragraph is to show how heretical statements were justified by v2. this serves not only to justify resistance to v2, but also once more to substantiate the fact of a severe church crisis. 4.4.1. continuance of the old covenant on the continuance of the old covenant, cantate domino says:[37] “it firmly believes, professes and teaches that the legal prescriptions of the old testament or the mosaic law, which are novus ordo (no) is the second point where the fsspx offers resistance. here too it must be examined whether this is justified. for this coming section i must first disclose that my argument, although internal discussion about whether the no should be called “intrinsically evil.” from my perspective this is a category mistake. only actions can be evil, so at most one could say that attending or especially if he does not usually attend the no but, for example, only does so while on vacation. leaving aside the discussion about “intrinsically evil,” the fsspx would certainly say that the no is schlecht?” and summarizes the core argument as follows:[52] original: “er ist schlecht, weil er 1.) den opfercharakter der messe und die transsubstantiation verdunkelt. ein messritus hat aber 87);” translation: “it belongs to the conferences of bishops to establish the adaptations indicated in this general instruction and in the ordo missae , and, after their recognition by the apostolic see, to introduce them into the missal. these are: [...] - texts of the chants at the entrance, at the presentation of the gifts, and at communion (cf. above, nos. 48, 74, 87);” the german bishops, for example, made use of this freedom. in die feier der gemeindemesse 87 there are now three options, and instead of the suscipiat one may alternatively pray:[61] original: “lasset uns beten zu gott, dem allmachtigen vater, dass er die gaben der kirche annehme zu seinem lob und zum heil der ganzen welt.” translation: “let us pray to god, the almighty father, that he may accept the gifts of the church for his praise and for the salvation of the whole world.” here again it is obvious how the sacrificial character is replaced by that of a meal. 5.1.4. conclusion we have now seen how father gaudron set up a valid argument from three premises and the conclusion “the no is bad in itself.” we defended the first two relatively uncontroversial premises and showed that some arguments also support the third premise, from which it would follow that the no is in fact bad in itself. 5.2. the moderate position as mentioned at the beginning, my position is somewhat different from that of the fsspx. more precisely, i see my position as the one the fsspx should adopt, because it brings together all of its basic assumptions in a logically consistent way. i would agree that the no is bad in itself insofar as it describes the mass as a rite, but i would also hold that not every mass celebrated according to the no rite is a bad mass. my analogy is that of a cookbook. a cookbook describes how a dish must be cooked, but it can also leave room for variation, and this room must remain within certain limits if the cookbook is to be good. if a cookbook allows the option of replacing salt with rat poison in its dishes, then it is a bad cookbook, because it leaves room outside the bounds of a good cookbook. however, this does not yet mean that all dishes prepared according to this cookbook are bad, since one can simply cook them with salt rather than rat poison. by this i am not saying that all problems with the no are purely accidental; the no clearly has protestantizing tendencies, as father gaudron’s examples show. but these are not sufficient to say that the sacrificial character is obscured. of a mass such as at the oxford oratory, celebrated in latin ad orientem , with communion only on the tongue and without replacing the suscipiat , one simply cannot say that the sacrificial character would not be clearly communicated.[62] father gaudron answers this: original: “auch bei der konservativsten form des nom finden sich der wegfall des offertoriums, der kniebeugen und segenszeichen. auch diese form stellt ein „auffalliges abrucken von der katholischen theologie der messe dar.“” translation: “even in the most conservative form of the nom one finds the disappearance of the offertory, the genuflections, and the signs of blessing. this form too represents a ‘striking departure from the catholic theology of the mass.’” he also gives further arguments against the best possible no. the problem is that they are all insufficient. they may well be true, but for his argument to work he would have to show that even the best possible no obscures the sacrificial character, and his arguments simply do not carry that far. if, however, one accepts my position that the no is bad in itself but that the individual mass can nevertheless be good, then all the pieces of the puzzle fit together. the first two uncontroversial premises remain the same; only the third is interpreted differently and can be defended much more easily. instead of having to show that the no obscures the sacrificial character, the burden of proof falls to showing only that the no leaves too much room to obscure the sacrificial character. now one can mention not only the essential deficiencies of the no listed by father gaudron, but also accidental properties such as: communion in the hand extraordinary ministers of communion ad populum the possibility of replacing the suscipiat if the premise is changed from “the no obscures the sacrificial character of the mass and does not make it clear” to “the no leaves too much room to obscure the sacrificial character of the mass and not make it clear,” the premise becomes hardly controversial for any conservative catholic. the second premise, “making clear and not obscuring the sacrificial character of the mass is an essential task of the mass,” remains untouched, because the no fails to fulfill this task simply by leaving this room. the first premise also remains untouched. the fsspx could also continue to maintain its principle of advising the faithful against attending the no, because the danger that the individual mass is also bad could still be judged too high. nor does my position really contradict the quotations from bishop lefebvre. for example, he says: original: “die sunde wird schwer, wenn eine informierte und gewarnte person trotzdem regelmassig dorthin geht und sagt: >mir ist es egal, ich furchte nicht um meinen glauben<, obwohl sie genau weiss, dass es gefahrlich ist” translation: “the sin becomes grave when an informed and warned person nevertheless goes there regularly and says, ‘i do not care; i do not fear for my faith,’ although he knows very well that it is dangerous.” one can continue to agree with this. it is simply a case-by-case judgment whether the person really thinks that the no is dangerous to his faith. the other quotation is the following: original: „wer nicht zu diesen messen gehen kann [gemeint ist die uberlieferte messe], soll sie sonntags in seinem messbuch lesen, wenn moglich innerhalb der familie, wie die christen in den missionslandern tun, die nur zwei- oder dreimal, manchmal nur einmal im jahr vom priester besucht werden.“ translation: “whoever cannot go to these masses [meaning the traditional mass] should read them on sundays in his missal, if possible within the family, as christians do in mission countries who are visited by a priest only two or three times, sometimes only once, a year.” one can also still agree with this quotation if it is interpreted as general pastoral advice that allows exceptions in individual cases, just as the fsspx already allows exceptions in individual cases, such as funerals of close relatives. the moderate position could be described with an adapted analogy of the catechism. we would no longer say, “a catechism is not only bad if it teaches falsehood, but also if it withholds something essential,” but would offer an analogy such as the following: “a curriculum in a catholic seminary that can be implemented correctly in such a way that the student ends up with a protestant understanding of theology is a bad curriculum, even if the curriculum also makes possible the teaching of a good course.” 5.3. does the moderate position justify resistance? the attentive reader will now object that the moderate position lowers the burden of proof, but at the same time also lowers the gravity of the consequences that can be drawn from it. let us take an atheist as an example. he would argue against any involvement of the church in political matters, since from his perspective the basis for the church’s position is grounded in a false belief. he might argue fanatically that the church has nothing to say about the morality of laws because its positions are derived from irrational, outdated positions in a man-made bible. an agnostic could now say, “hey, you can simply say that you do not know whether god exists. that lowers your burden of proof. you no longer need to present negative arguments against god, but only undermine the arguments for god.” the problem, however, is that the agnostic then has a much weaker argument against the church’s involvement in political questions. he can no longer invoke the claim that the church’s positions are derived from irrational, outdated positions in a man-made bible. he has to stay out of such claims because he does not claim to be able to answer such questions. at first glance, a similar dilemma follows from the moderate position on the no: if the no can also be celebrated in a way pleasing to god, how can one refuse to do it? the church and the pope fundamentally have the right to change the liturgy. if they were to introduce a heretical mass, one could of course resist it, but why also resist a rite that is potentially heretical yet can be celebrated orthodoxly? 5.3.1. disobedience to laws first, we want to look at the principle of why one can be disobedient to laws at all. the introduction of changes to the liturgy is not a dogmatic decision concerning faith or morals, but a disciplinary question. with fallible disciplinary decisions, as with every law, the principle lex injusta non obligat applies. st. thomas writes:[63] “on the other hand laws may be unjust in two ways: first, by being contrary to human good, through being opposed to the things mentioned above - either in respect of the end, as when an authority imposes on his subjects burdensome laws, conducive, not to the common good, but rather to his own cupidity or vainglory - or in respect of the author, as when a man makes a law that goes beyond the power committed to him - or in respect of the form, as when burdens are imposed unequally on the community, although with a view to the common good. the like are acts of violence rather than laws; because, as augustine says (de lib. arb. i, 5),”a law that is not just, seems to be no law at all.” wherefore such laws do not bind in conscience, except perhaps in order to avoid scandal or disturbance, for which cause a man should even yield his right, according to matthew 5:40-41: “if a man... take away thy coat, let go thy cloak also unto him; and whosoever will force thee one mile, go with him other two.”” an unjust law therefore does not bind, and for a law to be just it must serve the common good. does the no serve the common good? as we discussed above, the no as a rite is bad in itself because it specifically gives room to obscure the essence of the mass. that cannot serve the common good. georg may writes:[64] original: “nun ware es unzutreffend, zu behaupten, der ordo missae pauls vi. sei haretisch, wie es hie und da geschehen ist. haresie ist die harte leugnung von wahrheiten, die mit gottlichem und katholischem glauben anzunehmen sind (c. 1325 $ 2 cic). der neue ordo missae leugnet kein dogma der kirche. das schweigen von einer lehre ist nicht gleichbedeutend mit ihrer ablehnung. indes ist oben nachgewiesen worden, dass der ordo missae pauls vi. gegenuber dem ordo missae pius’ v., dogmatisch gesehen, einen ruckschritt darstellt, dass er glaube und frommigkeit des katholischen volkes erheblich weniger fordert, ja gefahrdet und dass er bedenkliche pastorale schaden herauffuhrt. das alles braucht hier nicht wiederholt denial of truths that must be accepted with divine and catholic faith (c. 1325 § 2 cic). the new ordo missae denies no dogma of the church. silence about a doctrine is not the same as its rejection. nevertheless, it has been demonstrated above that the ordo missae of paul vi, compared with the ordo missae of pius v, represents a regression from the dogmatic point of view; that it promotes the must be drawn from these facts. this conclusion can only be: since it is established that the ordo missae of paul vi does not correspond to the requirements that must be made of the unchanging parts of the holy mass; that it summons dangers of enormous scope; that, in short, it does not serve the common good of the church but harms it, it follows that the law introducing it is an unjust law. it has no binding force of itself. priests and faithful may disregard the law that prescribes the use of the ordo missae of paul vi. they may use it if the harms arising from non-use would be greater, for example if priests would certainly lose their position by not using it and their faithful would thereby either be left orphaned or handed over to a progressive ‘parish leader.’ their conscience will have to decide what responsibility for faith, worship, and pastoral care demands.” 5.3.2. justification of the fsspx since the introduction of the no does not serve the common good and is therefore an unjust law, the fsspx is free to refuse obedience to this law. this holds even if one adopts the moderate position. nevertheless, beyond this, a justification is still needed insofar as even unjust laws bind to the extent required to avoid scandal or disorder. the justification here is that the celebration of and participation in the no is, to a certain degree, an assent to the underlying heretical theology. father gaudron writes with respect to the best possible no masses:[52] original: “bei der beurteilung des nom muss man das ganze messbuch vor augen haben, und hier findet sich eben nicht nur eine konservative form mit romischem kanon, sondern ganz gleichberechtigt die moglichkeit, die messe so zu feiern, dass sie von einer protestantischen abendmahlsfeier kaum unterscheidbar ist. man kann ja auch nicht behaupten, die bucher eines hans kung seien an sich gut, weil sich auf einigen seiten auch richtige und schone gedanken neben den haresien befinden. wer die neue messe annimmt, gibt damit seine grundsatzliche zustimmung zur ganzen liturgiereform, selbst wenn er den nom personlich nur in einer konservativen form feiert.” translation: “in judging the nom, one must keep the whole missal in view, and here one finds not only a conservative form with the roman canon, but, on fully equal footing, the possibility of celebrating the mass in such a way that it is hardly distinguishable from a protestant lord’s supper service. after all, one cannot claim that the books of a hans kung are good in themselves because correct and beautiful thoughts are found on some pages alongside the heresies. whoever accepts the new mass thereby gives his fundamental assent to the entire liturgical reform, even if he personally celebrates the nom only in a conservative form.” the application to the individual will certainly differ from person to person. as described in the preceding quotation from georg may, in the current church crisis it is the right decision for some pastors to celebrate the no. in my assessment, it is also generally better for the faithful to attend the no on sundays than no mass at all. but this too depends on the circumstances. i basically agree with the fsspx that participation in the no should be passive, precisely in order to avoid giving full outward assent or acceptance to the liturgical reform and thereby causing scandal. however, this attitude can also be expressed in individual cases even when one participates actively, for example if one is the only person who receives communion on the tongue and deliberately goes not to an extraordinary minister of communion but to the pastor. for the fsspx, however, the situation is different. both at the time of its introduction and today, celebration of the no by its priests would clearly signal outwardly that the dogmatic objections raised are no longer maintained. it would be a clearly scandalous assent to the underlying false image of the essence of the mass, and therefore it must be avoided uncompromisingly. i want to explain this more concretely in what follows. 5.3.3. the concept of scandal in thomas and the fsspx thomas defines scandal in st ii-ii q.43 a.1 as: “dictum vel factum minus rectum praebens alteri occasionem ruinae”: a word or action less rightly done that gives another occasion for ruin. the decisive word here is dictum - word, statement. thomas means by this that an action can have a communicative character. it says something, even if it explicitly asserts nothing. the scandal then lies not only in the action itself, but in what it means to the observer. thomas further distinguishes between active scandal ( scandalum datum ) and passive scandal ( scandalum acceptum ). for our question, only active scandal is relevant: the giver of the action is responsible for the confusion he causes. now we want to show that celebration of the no by fsspx priests would be active scandal in the thomistic sense. the argument has three steps: 5.3.3.1. first step: the action has a communicative character for decades the fsspx has maintained a clearly articulated dogmatic position on the no. this position is public, institutional, and inseparably connected with the name of the fsspx. as a result, every action of an fsspx priest with respect to the no necessarily has semantic content: it is not a neutral liturgical act, but an implicit statement about the validity of the objections raised. if an fsspx priest celebrates the no, he does not merely say: “i consider this rite suboptimal, but i celebrate it anyway.” whether he wants to or not, he says: “the dogmatic objections for which my community stands no longer hold.” this is a dictum in the thomistic sense - a statement through action. 5.3.3.2. second step: this statement gives occasion for spiritual ruin first it must be emphasized that the scandal is not limited to the circle of fsspx supporters. because the action has a communicative character, its statement is directed to everyone who perceives it and knows the position of the fsspx. what it communicates is an objectively false proposition: that a publicly advanced, dogmatically grounded criticism that has never been substantively refuted may be abandoned under institutional pressure. this is scandalum datum in the strict sense, active scandal, because the action itself says something wrong, regardless of who receives it. it suggests that truth yields to authority, and this is precisely the basic modernist movement against which the entire resistance is directed. the scandal here is therefore not fed by a self-created expectation, but by the objective situation: a true and unanswered criticism that would be revoked. beyond this, especially grave harm is done to that group which has entrusted itself to the fsspx precisely because of the dogmatic seriousness of its position. on the basis of fsspx teaching, these faithful have developed a certain understanding of the mass, an awareness of the sacrificial character and of the protestantizing tendencies of the no rite. if the fsspx priest now celebrates the no, they will either conclude that the objections were not so serious after all and abandon their dogmatic vigilance, which is a real spiritual harm, or fall into deep confusion about the essence of the mass, likewise a spiritual harm. both correspond exactly to what thomas calls ruina spiritualis : not necessarily a formal sin, but a real regression in faith. 5.3.3.3. third step: it is scandalum pusillorum in q.43 a.7, thomas distinguishes between the scandal of the weak ( pusilli ) and the scandal of the pharisees. the scandal of the pharisees - that is, scandal arising from malice or narrow-mindedness - need not be avoided if doing so would come at the expense of truth. the scandal of the weak, however, must be avoided even when the action itself would be permitted. thomas writes: original: “sicut augustinus dicit [...] debemus temporalia relinquere propter scandalum vitandum” translation: “as augustine says, [...] we must give up temporal goods in order to avoid scandal.” the faithful of the fsspx and all observers are here the pusilli in the theological sense - not because they are stupid, but because in a church crisis they depend on the leadership of the fsspx to preserve their faith in the sacrifice of the mass. an fsspx that celebrates the no takes this leadership away from them. 5.3.3.4. a self-made problem? one might perhaps object that this is therefore a home-made problem. if the fsspx had not resisted, it would not have to resist. but this ignores the fact that the resistance was necessary from the beginning, as shown, among other things, by the fact that the heretical formula in igmr 7 was softened. 5.4. conclusion let us summarize the argument. the starting point was father gaudron’s formal argument: because a rite essentially has the task of making clear the essence of the mass, and because the no fails precisely in this task, it is bad in itself. the first two premises, the thomistic definition of evil as privation and the determination of the mass supported by trent and mediator dei , are hardly disputable. only the third premise is contested. in the moderate position, i proposed weakening this third premise: it is enough to show that the no leaves too much room to obscure the sacrificial character. this formulation is supported by the protestantizing tendencies, the original igmr definition, the arbitrariness regarding the suscipiat , ad populum celebration, communion in the hand, and extraordinary ministers of communion, and it nevertheless leads to the same result: the no as a rite is bad in itself, even if an individual mass celebrated according to it can be good. but that does not yet decide the matter, because a rite bad in itself could nevertheless be legitimately prescribed by the church. here, however, the principle lex injusta non obligat applies: a law that prescribes a rite that does not serve the common good of the church is not binding. georg may showed this in detail. this argument is independent of the fsspx; it applies to every priest and every member of the faithful who accepts the above premises. the question whether one may resist is therefore objectively answered. what remains is only the question how far this resistance must go. in principle, a broad spectrum can be legitimate here: from the priest who, according to georg may’s standard, continues to celebrate the no in order not to abandon his faithful to progressive parish leaders, all the way to complete refusal. for the fsspx, however, the situation is no longer an open weighing of options. the dogmatic objections that support its resistance were substantively justified from the beginning, as even the later softening of the heretical igmr definition shows. as long as they have not been answered, every celebration of the no by fsspx priests would not mean “reconciliation,” but the revocation of a criticism that has never been refuted, and thus would spiritually harm precisely those faithful who have relied on the seriousness of this criticism ( scandalum pusillorum in the sense of st ii-ii q.43). the refusal to celebrate the no is therefore not disobedience out of narrow-mindedness. it follows from two steps valid for all catholics: the rite fails to fulfill an essential task, and the law prescribing it therefore does not bind; and from a third step that arises only in the concrete situation of the fsspx, but precisely there because the underlying criticism is substantively correct and not because it was once loudly voiced. 6. the announced consecrations finally, we now want to examine whether the illicit episcopal consecrations are also justified. just because the refusal to sign v2 is justified and the refusal to celebrate the no is justified, it does not yet follow that the illicit episcopal consecration is justified too. may one violate the prohibition? is the requirement of the pope’s consent divine law? are such consecrations necessarily schismatic? do they automatically lead to excommunication? these are the questions i want to answer here. 6.1. illicit episcopal consecrations in canon law canon 1013 says:[65] original: “keinem bischof ist es gestattet, jemanden zum bischof zu weihen, wenn nicht zuvor der papstliche auftrag feststeht.” translation: “no bishop is permitted to consecrate anyone a bishop unless it is first established that there is a pontifical mandate.” what, then, justifies violating this canon law? we can approach this question from two distinct but nevertheless related legal principles: the principle of epikie and the maxim necessitas legem non habet . 6.1.1. epikie epikie (from greek επιεικεια, forbearance, leniency), one of the oldest virtues, according to st. thomas:[66] original: “die habituelle bereitschaft, die inneren u. ausseren, oft aussergewohnl. umstande genau abzuwagen u. eine handlung im lichte der den einzelnormen ubergeordneten eth. prinzipien zu beurteilen”. translation: “the habitual readiness to weigh carefully the inner and outer, often extraordinary circumstances and to judge an action in the light of the ethical principles superior to the individual norms.” in short, epikie is the principle of disregarding the letter of a law in individual cases when obeying the law in that individual case would contradict the purpose of the law. st. thomas permits the application of this principle in cases:[67] original: “in denen die wortliche befolgung des gesetzes verwerflich ware, (...) moglicherweise auch in anderen fallen, in denen der gesetzgeber nicht bereit ware, den untertanen zu binden, wenn er selbst anwesend ware.” translation: “in which literal observance of the law would be blameworthy, (...) possibly also in other cases in which the legislator would not be willing to bind the subject if he himself were present.” for st. thomas, the justification for epikie results from the fact that the legislator cannot foresee all individual circumstances and therefore must issue laws that cover the supermajority of cases.[68] this makes clear that when st. thomas speaks of the “legislator (...) being present,” he means the original legislator, and not necessarily the current holder of legislative authority. the latter could reinterpret and abuse the intention of the law. his example is the following:[69] original: “das gesetz besagt, dass ein hinterlegter gegenstand zuruckgegeben werden muss, wenn der eigentumer ihn verlangt. befindet sich der besitzer einer waffe jedoch in einem wutanfall, wenn er sie zuruckfordert, und besteht die ernsthafte gefahr, dass er jemanden verletzen konnte, ist es nicht richtig, sich an die norm zu halten. in diesem fall ist es angebracht, das gesetz zu ignorieren und dem sogenannten „gerechtigkeitssinn“ zu folgen.” translation: “the law states that a deposited object must be returned when its owner asks for it. if, however, the owner of a weapon is in a fit of rage when he asks for it back, and there is serious danger that he could injure someone, it is not right to adhere to the norm. in this case it is appropriate to ignore the law and to follow the so-called ‘sense of justice.’” epikie applies to all human positive law, both civil and ecclesiastical.[70] how can this principle now be applied to the case of the fsspx? the prohibition of illicit episcopal consecrations as it stands today in canon law was formulated under john paul ii. canon 1387 says:[71] original: “ein bischof, der jemanden ohne papstlichen auftrag zum bischof weiht, und ebenso, wer von ihm die weihe empfangt, ziehen sich die dem apostolischen stuhl vorbehaltene exkommunikation als tatstrafe zu.” translation: “a bishop who consecrates someone a bishop without a pontifical mandate, and likewise the person who receives the consecration from him, incurs a latae sententiae excommunication reserved to the apostolic see.” but this is not the origin of the law. its origin lies in the investiture controversy, in which pope gregory vii in dictatus papae first claimed the exclusive right to appoint bishops. he wrote literally:[72] original: “dass er allein bischofe absetzen und wieder einsetzen kann.” translation: “that he alone can depose and reinstate bishops.” several hundred years later, it was first written into canon law by pope benedict xv. there canon 953 still said: “the consecration of a bishop is reserved to the roman pontiff so that it is not permitted to any bishop to consecrate another as bishop without first having gotten a pontifical mandate.” canon 2370 then says:[73] “a bishop consecrating another bishop, and the assistant bishops or, in the place of bishops, priests, and those who receive consecration without an apostolic mandate against the prescription of canon 953 are by the law suspended until the apostolic see dispenses them” this prohibition is then condemned once more in the magisterium under pius xii, who writes in ad apostolorum principis (aap) 39:[74] “granted this exception, it follows that bishops who have been neither named nor confirmed by the apostolic see, but who, on the contrary, have been elected and consecrated in defiance of its express orders, enjoy no powers of teaching or of jurisdiction since jurisdiction passes to bishops only through the roman pontiff as we admonished in the encyclical letter mystici corporis in the following words:”... as far as his own diocese is concerned each (bishop) feeds the flock entrusted to him as a true shepherd and rules it in the name of christ. yet in exercising this office they are not altogether independent but are subordinate to the lawful authority of the roman pontiff, although enjoying ordinary power of jurisdiction which they receive directly from the same supreme pontiff.”” in order to apply the principle of epikie to the consecrations of the fsspx, we must first ask who the legislator is. as we have seen above, this is not about the current holder of legislative power but about the original legislator. since the canon under john paul ii only changed the penalty for illicit episcopal consecration, but not the prohibition as such, we can regard benedict xv as the original legislator. for even though the new canon law replaces the old and draws its legitimacy fundamentally from the authority of the pope, it nevertheless refers to the 1917 code of canon law when it says in canon 6: original: “die canones dieses codex sind, soweit sie altes recht wiedergeben, auch unter berucksichtigung der kanonischen tradition zu wurdigen.” translation: “the canons of this code, insofar as they reproduce old law, are also to be assessed with due regard for canonical tradition.” the new canon law is therefore also to be seen as a continuation of the old canon law, to be read in its tradition, though of course where there are contradictions it is not bound by the old law. insofar as it is to be understood in this way, benedict xv can therefore be regarded as the legislator of the prohibition, even though john paul ii adjusted the associated penalty. one can now ask whether benedict xv, had he been present in the case of the fsspx episcopal consecrations, would have approved the non-application of his law, since it represents an unforeseen consequence of his law in an individual case. here it must be mentioned that the codification of the prohibition, as previously noted, goes back to condemnations by earlier popes who acted in the context of state interference in church affairs. it was not developed in the context of internal church conflicts and was only later applied to them. benedict xv condemned modernism in his encyclical ad beatissimi apostolorum (aba) 25 and wrote:[75] “hence arose the monstrous errors of”modernism,” which our predecessor rightly declared to be “the synthesis of all heresies,” and solemnly condemned. we hereby renew that condemnation in all its fulness, venerable brethren, and as the plague is not yet entirely stamped out, but lurks here and there in hidden places, we exhort all to be carefully here and there in hidden places, we exhort all to be carefully on their guard against any contagion of the evil, to which we may apply the words job used in other circumstances: “it is a fire that devoureth even to destruction, and rooteth up all things that spring” ( job xxxi. 12). nor do we merely desire that catholics should shrink from the errors of modernism, but also from the tendencies or what is called the spirit of modernism. those who are infected by that spirit develop a keen dislike for all that savours of antiquity and become eager searchers after novelties in everything: in the way in which they carry out religious functions, in the ruling of catholic institutions, and even in private exercises of piety. therefore it is our will that the law of our forefathers should still be held sacred: “let there be no innovation; keep to what has been handed down.”” thus, if one considers that benedict xv strongly condemned the modernism that entered through v2, and if one considers that his prohibition of illicit episcopal consecrations arises from the investiture controversy and not from internal church conflicts, we have a good basis for assuming that he would approve the non-application of his law to this individual case, because at the time he enacted the law he could not foresee such a case. we can summarize the argument from epikie as follows: the prohibition of illicit episcopal consecrations has an identifiable legislative history with an identifiable purpose : to protect the church from the usurpation of the episcopal office by external powers. from gregory vii through trent to benedict xv, the context is consistent: investiture controversy, state-church systems, josephinism, communist interference. the legislator wanted to prevent secular power from deciding over the occupation of episcopal sees. the fsspx situation is structurally inverse: here a bishop consecrates without a pontifical mandate not to serve an external power, but to preserve the received order of the church against a perceived internal deviation. this constellation - an internal church conflict over tradition in which the governing authority itself appears as the problem - is simply absent from the legislative tradition of the prohibition. the decisive thomistic point is then this: the legislator benedict xv cannot have willed, in concreto , that his prohibition should apply precisely when its actual protective purpose - the preservation of the episcopal office in its received form - is at stake. to apply the law literally here produces an outcome that contradicts the spirit of the law. and that is the classic case of epikie . the fact that john paul ii explicitly refused the mandate does not necessarily weaken the argument, because for epikie what is decisive is not the current expression of will of the lawgiver, but the original intention of the law. if the current holder of legislative power applies the law in a way that contradicts its own history of origin, then this is precisely the case in which epikie applies - and not the case in which it is excluded. 6.1.2. necessitas legem non habet the second legal principle under which we can place the consecrations of the fsspx is the maxim necessitas legem non habet , that is, “necessity has no law.” unlike epikie , this is not about interpreting a law against its letter in the sense of the legislator’s intention, that is, not about an operation within the legal order, but about the priority of a higher norm over positive law. epikie applies the law, only not according to its letter. necessitas suspends the binding force of the law because a good standing above it is at stake. thomas treats the principle using the classic example of theft from hunger in st ii-ii q.66 a.7 . there he asks whether someone in a state of necessity may take another’s property, and answers in the affirmative:[76] “nevertheless, if the need be so manifest and urgent, that it is evident that the present need must be remedied by whatever means be at hand (for instance when a person is in some imminent danger, and there is no other possible remedy), then it is lawful for a man to succor his own need by means of another’s property, by taking it either openly or secretly: nor is this properly speaking theft or robbery.” this is the clean necessitas structure. the right of property remains intact as a norm and is not reinterpreted. what happens is that, in this concrete situation, it yields to a higher norm: the protection of life, which follows from natural law itself. thomas formulates the general principle at the end of st i-ii q.96 a.6 in the classic maxim necessitas non habet legem .[77] necessitas is therefore not a component of positive law that the respective legal community could establish or abolish at will, but a priority rule standing above positive law, following from natural law and from the essence of human legislation. it is meta-juridical in the strict sense: it operates above positive law and determines when positive law must yield. in canon law, this priority finds its most prominent expression in canon 1752, the final canon of the 1983 cic: salus animarum, quae in ecclesia suprema semper lex esse debet , the salvation of souls must always be the supreme law in the church.[78] this canon determines what applies in conflicts between positive church laws and higher goods. if a positive law does not promote the salvation of souls but endangers it, then it must yield. that is exactly the canonical form of the necessitas principle. let us apply this to the episcopal consecrations of the fsspx. the prohibition of consecration without a pontifical mandate is positive church law. it is not divine law, as we will show in the next section, and therefore falls under the necessitas rule. the question is therefore whether in 1988 there was a state of necessity that endangered the good of “the salvation of souls” so gravely that the positive prohibition had to yield. the necessity relevant here is not the preservation of a rite or of a liturgical style, but the modernist crisis itself discussed in the preceding sections. if pius x is right that modernism is the “synthesis of all heresies,” and if the indicators collected in the preceding sections are correct - the voting behavior of the german bishops, the state of belief among clergy according to studies, the ambiguities embedded in v2 in dh, lg xvi, and lg viii and their reception, the structural problems of the no, the absence of canonical reactions against bishops and theologians teaching modernistically - then this is a situation in which the salvation of souls is endangered systematically and over generations. this is necessity in the technical sense, because the one good to which the church is ultimately obliged is placed at stake by the failure of her own disciplinary and doctrinal structures. this brings us to the decisive counter-question. in eda of july 2, 1988, john paul ii expressly denied the existence of a state of necessity:[79] “in particular, one cannot affirm a ‘state of necessity’, by which anyone would be permitted to confer episcopal ordination contrary to the will of the supreme pontiff, supreme pastor of the universal church.” is the discussion thereby ended? not if one takes seriously the specific nature of this judgment. the statement “there is no state of necessity” is not a magisterial judgment about faith or morals, but a factual determination about the concrete situation of the church. it therefore does not fall under the conditions of papal infallibility as the first vatican council explicitly outlined them in pastor aeternus , chapter 4 (ds 3074): original: “der romische bischof besitzt, wenn er ex cathedra spricht, das heisst, wenn er, das amt des hirten und lehrers aller christen ausubend, kraft seiner hochsten apostolischen autoritat eine lehre uber glauben oder sitten als von der ganzen kirche festzuhaltende definiert, durch den gottlichen beistand, der ihm im seligen petrus verheissen ist, jene unfehlbarkeit, mit der der gottliche erloser seine kirche bei der definition einer lehre uber glauben oder sitten ausgestattet wissen wollte.” translation: “the roman pontiff possesses, when he speaks ex cathedra , that is, when, exercising the office of shepherd and teacher of all christians, by virtue of his supreme apostolic authority, he defines a doctrine concerning faith or morals to be held by the whole church, through the divine assistance promised to him in blessed peter, that infallibility with which the divine redeemer willed his church to be endowed in defining doctrine concerning faith or morals.” three conditions are named here: an ex cathedra act, doctrine concerning faith or morals, and proposal for acceptance by the whole church. eda is a motu proprio with disciplinary and fact-finding character and fulfills none of them. ott confirms this a contrario in his fundamentals of catholic dogma when he states:[80] “the ordinary and usual form of the papal teaching activity is not infallible. further, the decisions of the roman congregations (holy office, bible commission) are not infallible.” if even the ordinary papal magisterium in the narrower sense is not infallible, then still less is a determination about the ecclesial situation embedded in a disciplinary act. a critic might object here that papal infallibility must be extended beyond faith and morals to disciplinary factual judgments of this kind, because otherwise precisely that private jurisdiction arises against which we want to guard. but this extension itself is not supported by the magisterium. whoever wanted to extend infallibility to such judgments would burst the limits formulated in pastor aeternus and thereby introduce a new doctrine for which there is no support in the magisterium. that papal factual and disciplinary judgments could very well err in church history is shown by two precedents already partly addressed in the preceding sections. the first is the arian crisis. athanasius resisted not only an overwhelming majority of bishops and a pope yielding under pressure; he effectively resisted the factual assessment prevailing in the hierarchy at that time, and he had no basis for this other than his own judgment about the theological and ecclesial situation. had he asked liberius in exile at beroea whether there was a state of necessity justifying his resistance, he would hardly have received an affirmative answer. athanasius was later canonized. the second and structurally even more fitting precedent is eusebius of dorylaeum. around christmas 428, shortly after patriarch nestorius had rejected the title theotokos for the virgin mary in a sermon, eusebius, then still a layman, lawyer, and agens in rebus at the imperial court in constantinople, stood up in the middle of the liturgy and publicly contradicted him with the confession that the eternal word, begotten before all ages, had also submitted himself to the second birth according to the flesh (cf. cyril of alexandria, adv. nestor. i, 20, pg 76, 41d; marius mercator, liber subnotationum , pl 48, 769b). shortly thereafter he circulated in the city the contestatio pamphlet (cpg 5940/8620), in which he compared nestorius with paul of samosata.[81] what is decisive for our argument is that eusebius took this step without consulting a higher authority . at that time he had neither episcopal nor teaching authority; he was a layman and based his resistance solely on his own judgment about the theological situation against the reigning patriarch of one of the most important episcopal sees of christendom. nor did he have the excuse that no higher authority was reachable. pope celestine i resided in rome and was orthodox. eusebius could theoretically have turned to him and asked for an assessment of the situation. he did not do so. the formal accusation against nestorius before celestine was later pursued not by eusebius but chiefly by cyril of alexandria (cf. cyril’s epistula ad coelestinum , aco i,1,5). eusebius himself acted before and independently of this higher involvement. strictly speaking, eusebius did not violate positive law, but publicly contradicted his bishop. his case is therefore not a direct necessitas versus law case in the narrow sense. what it does show, however, is precisely the contested point of our argument: that the judgment “there is an ecclesial state of necessity” is not the privilege of the highest authority and does not presuppose its prior confirmation. eusebius made such a factual determination independently as a layman, and the church confirmed it retroactively and even explicitly. this confirmation is not only structural, through the later condemnation of nestorius, but also direct in the papal word. on august 11, 430, in his epistola xiv ad clerum et populum constantinopolitanum , that is, before the council of ephesus, celestine writes expressly to the constantinopolitan laity and clergy who resisted nestorius, and calls their situation blessed precisely when they themselves must judge their pasture because the shepherd has become a wolf:[82] original: “quid spei habeat grex, quando lupum se ipse pastor ostendit, et sic oves invadit, ut grassetur in singulas? (...) beatus tamen grex cui dedit dominus de pascuis judicare.” (pl 50, 505) translation: “what hope has the flock when the shepherd himself shows himself to be a wolf and invades the sheep so as to rage against each one? (...) yet blessed is the flock to whom the lord has given to judge concerning the pastures.” (pl 50, 505) but celestine goes further. he explicitly places athanasius before the resisters as an example: original: “habetis vos quicumque ecclesia estis ejecti, pene nostrorum temporum beatae recordationis athanasii alexandrinae ecclesiae prudentissimi sacerdotis exemplum. cui non consolationi sit illius tolerantia? cui non sit exemplo illius fortitudo?” (pl 50, 509) translation: “you, whoever have been cast out of the church, have almost in our own times the example of athanasius of blessed memory, the most prudent priest of the church of alexandria. to whom is his endurance not a consolation? to whom is his courage not an example?” (pl 50, 509) and finally he declares the canonical sanctions with which nestorius had punished the resisters - removals from office, excommunications - to be retroactively null: original: “aperte sedis nostrae sanxit auctoritas, nullum sive episcopum, sive clericum, seu professione aliqua christianum, qui a nestorio vel ejus similibus, ex quo talia praedicare coeperunt, vel loco suo vel communione dejecti sunt, vel ejectum vel excommunicatum videri.” (pl 50, 510) translation: “the authority of our see has openly decreed that no bishop, cleric, or christian of any profession who, by nestorius or by those like him, since they began to preach such things, has been cast down from his place or communion, is to be regarded as deposed or excommunicated.” (pl 50, 510) this is not only structural but explicit papal confirmation. the judgment of the laity and clergy in constantinople about the situation of their church, made without prior consultation with rome, was correct. the canonical sanctions imposed on them by the competent hierarchy for it were null. eusebius himself later became bishop of dorylaeum and was honored at the council of chalcedon in 451 as a defender of orthodoxy, in whose acts he brings the accusation against eutyches (aco ii,1,1). both precedents, athanasius and eusebius, therefore show structurally the same thing: the judgment about the existence of an ecclesial state of necessity is not reserved exclusively to the highest authority, at least not when that authority itself is compromised by political pressure (liberius under the arian emperor) or by theological decay (nestorius as patriarch, and in father schmidberger’s diagnosis the modernist basic attitudes of today’s popes). in both cases, judgment was made against the institutional tendency and without prior confirmation from above, and in both cases the church later explicitly confirmed the judgments. that resistance could in fact be offered independently of rome is, in the case of athanasius, explainable because of the possibility of consulting liberius only by the compromised state of that authority; in the case of eusebius it is even clearer, because an orthodox higher authority existed in rome to whom he could have turned, yet he still saw himself compelled to an independent judgment. this brings us to the last and weightiest objection, that of private jurisdiction. the critic says: if i can decide for myself whether to obey law x, why not every law? father schmidberger admitted in a personal conversation that the necessitas argument structurally does indeed open this door. but the answer does not lie in closing this door in principle, for this is precisely the whole point of the doctrine of necessitas ; rather, it lies in the theological and epistemological justification for why one must pass through it here and how one prevents this from collapsing into arbitrariness. first, thomas teaches that conscience binds absolutely, even an erroneous conscience, because human judgment is fundamentally required in every moral question (cf. st i-ii q.19 a.5). this does not lead to relativism, because conscience must be ordered to the objective moral law; it is only an expression of our epistemic finitude. christ did not grant his church infallibility in every act, but only under the precisely defined conditions listed by pastor aeternus . outside these conditions we must judge according to our best conscience and can err in doing so. the same applies to every necessitas judgment. it can be mistaken, but it can also be correct, and the possibility of error does not abolish the principle. the later ecclesial confirmation did not make the resistance of athanasius and eusebius correct retroactively; it merely showed it to have been correct. the act was already right or wrong at the moment of action, independently of whether and when a judgment from above followed. two things follow from this. first, the absence of such confirmation in the case of the fsspx says nothing about the rightness of its action, but only something about our present certainty regarding it. second, no objection can be built from this that makes prior confirmation a condition of permitted action. whoever demands that falls into an infinite regress: if the individual may never judge for himself whether a situation exists, then one authority would have to determine that it exists, another that this determination is correct, and so on. even the act by which a believer recognizes which authority is the legitimate magisterium at all is such an act of personal judgment (the classical praeambula fidei ). the possibility of independent judgment therefore cannot be denied without falling into epistemic nihilism. the question is never whether the individual judges, but only how high the threshold lies at which his judgment outweighs the presumption in favor of authority, and precisely this threshold is set high by the conditions named above: qualified competence, gravity of the situation, proportionality. second: the salvation of souls stands above all human laws, and we have no guarantee from christ that positive church law can never contradict this higher law. pastor aeternus promised infallibility to the church only in a clearly circumscribed domain, and disciplinary individual decisions and factual determinations about the situation of the church do not belong to this domain. whoever claims that the pope cannot err in the question whether a state of necessity exists extends infallibility beyond what the magisterium itself claims. incidentally, this is precisely the error against which donum veritatis warns under the heading of avoiding maximalism. third, and this is the decisive empirical point: if the necessitas argument really tipped over into private jurisdiction, this would show itself in the practice of the fsspx. it does not show itself. the fsspx draws clear boundaries that it does not overstep. it does not celebrate the still older holy week rite from the time before pius xii, although it prefers it liturgical-historically, because it acknowledges that this reform alone does not yet establish a state of necessity justifying such resistance. it claims no territorial jurisdiction, asserts no power of suspension over other clergy, and otherwise keeps the list of conciliar texts it rejects deliberately narrow. whoever had truly tipped over into private jurisdiction would not maintain such self-limitation. the question of proportionality remains. a state of necessity justifies only the minimal intervention needed to deal with it. were the episcopal consecrations in 1988 this minimal intervention? here the canonically recognized alternatives must be examined. the ecclesia dei communities such as the fssp and icksp can preserve the traditional liturgy, but they are bound to full acceptance of vatican ii and cannot publicly criticize the problematic texts from dh, lg xvi, and lg viii as contradicting tradition. but whoever wants to address the modernist crisis at the root must do exactly that. silent resistance within the existing structures fails even more fundamentally because it cannot be extended to priestly formation. without independent traditional seminaries, and without bishops who supervise these seminaries and ordain new priests, tradition breaks off over two generations. the episcopal consecrations of 1988 were therefore not an addition to the resistance, but its actual foundation, because they made it reproducible beyond lefebvre’s death. if one takes the state of necessity seriously as a diagnosis, then the consecrations were the proportionally minimal answer, not maximalism. 6.1.3. conclusion on canon law we have therefore seen that there are two established meta-juridical principles that can be applied to the fsspx episcopal consecrations and justify not submitting to canon law in this case. whether epikie is actually applicable in this case is certainly disputable. one can argue about whether benedict xv is in fact the relevant legislator and whether he would have permitted the fsspx episcopal consecrations as an individual exception. but because a good argument can be made for this, it should at least be mentioned here, even if this question probably cannot be settled definitively. the more relevant argument is necessitas , because this is the justification on which the fsspx itself relies. for that reason i defended this argument more extensively, and we have reached the conclusion that it is in fact successful. 6.2. is the prohibition not divine law? epikie and necessitas both apply only if the law in question is not divine law. but this is precisely what some critics claim. in my opinion, this understanding rests on a false post-conciliar view that episcopal consecration necessarily also brings jurisdiction with it. that this is not the case, that permission for episcopal consecrations is therefore not divine law, and that epikie and necessitas therefore apply, is what i want to defend in what follows. 6.2.1. why believe it is divine law? why should anyone think at all that it is divine law that the pope must permit episcopal consecrations? the statement is not found in the bible; if anything, it is not directly revealed divine law. if it is divine law, then it would have to be implicit in revelation. take papal infallibility as an example: a very new dogma, never clearly proclaimed in revelation. that it is nevertheless implicit in revelation is found by asking whether denying a statement leads to denying an already clearly formulated doctrine. in the case of the pope’s infallibility, one will find that if one denies this doctrine, one must either deny that the church can be infallible or deny that the pope is the head of the church. if one is logically consistent, then denying papal infallibility leads to denying less disputed doctrines. the situation is analogous with the claim that the necessity of papal permission for the consecration of bishops (npewb) is divine law. here the argument is that whoever rejects npewb also rejects the pope’s universal jurisdiction. this reasoning is also found in the best-known proof text for npewb, the encyclical ad apostolorum principis (aap), where pius xii quotes his letter ad sinarum gentem (asg) as follows:[83] “the power of jurisdiction which is conferred directly by divine right on the supreme pontiff comes to bishops by that same right, but only through the successor of peter, to whom not only the faithful but also all bishops are bound to be constantly subject and to adhere both by the reverence of obedience and by the bond of unity.” npewb as divine law therefore rests on the universal jurisdictional power of the pope, which was formulated most clearly in pastor aeternus (pa), where chapter 3 says:[84] original: “wenn also jemand sagt, der romische papst habe nur das amt der aufsicht oder der leitung, nicht aber die volle und hochste jurisdiktionsgewalt uber die gesamte kirche, nicht bloss in sachen des glaubens und der sitten, sondern auch in sachen, welche die disziplin und regierung der uber den ganzen erdkreis verbreiteten kirche betreffen; oder derselbe habe nur den vorzuglicheren anteil, nicht aber die ganze fulle dieser hochsten gewalt; oder diese seine gewalt sei nicht eine ordentliche und unmittelbare, sei es uber alle und die einzelnen kirchen oder uber und die einzelnen hirten und glaubigen, so sei er im banne.” translation: “therefore, if anyone says that the roman pontiff has only the office of inspection or direction, but not full and supreme jurisdictional power over the whole church, not only in matters of faith and morals, but also in those matters which concern the discipline and government of the church spread throughout the whole world; or that he has only the more important part, but not the whole fullness of this supreme power; or that this power of his is not ordinary and immediate, whether over all and each of the churches or over all and each of the pastors and faithful, let him be anathema.” the argument is therefore that whoever rejects npewb as divine law also rejects the pope’s universal jurisdictional power, which pa explicitly condemns. 6.2.2. episcopal consecration and jurisdictional power the question now is whether the consecration of bishops necessarily arrogates jurisdiction. if this is not the case, then it follows that npewb is divine law only when jurisdiction is also conferred, but otherwise only ecclesiastical positive law. lg 21 does indeed teach:[85] original: “die bischofsweihe ubertragt mit dem amt der heiligung auch die amter der lehre und der leitung” translation: “episcopal consecration confers, together with the office of sanctifying, also the offices of teaching and governing.” the problem with this, however, is that it is itself an innovation of v2 that contradicts tradition. pius xii teaches the exact opposite in asg 12 when he writes:[86] “by virtue of god’s will, the faithful are divided into two classes: the clergy and the laity. by virtue of the same will is established the twofold sacred hierarchy, namely, of orders and jurisdiction. besides - as has also been divinely established - the power of orders (through which the ecclesiastical hierarchy is composed of bishops, priests, and ministers) comes from receiving the sacrament of holy orders. but the power of jurisdiction, which is conferred upon the supreme pontiff directly by divine rights, flows to the bishops by the same right, but only through the successor of st. peter, to whom not only the simple faithful, but even all the bishops must be constantly subject, and to whom they must be bound by obedience and with the bond of unity.” the statement from lg is therefore only another example of a clear contradiction with tradition. that lg is false is also shown by classic examples of bishops without jurisdiction: auxiliary bishops: they help the diocesan bishop with ceremonial tasks such as ordinations and confirmations, but possess no proper authority over the faithful of the diocese. titular bishops: they symbolically receive the title of a defunct diocese, for example in north africa, but exercise no authority there. bishops emeriti: in modern law, bishops resign their jurisdiction at the age of 75, but remain bishops by their consecration. ratzinger himself admits this innovation when he says: ” indeed, the rigid dividing line that had stood for centuries in the minds of most western theologians between the power of order and the power of jurisdiction is now becoming surmountable,” ( la collegialite: developpement theologique in l’eglise de vatican ii , vol. 3, cerf, collection unam sanctam , 51c, p. 751, quoted in [87]) this new understanding is also reflected in the new canon law, where the prohibition moved from the section “offenses against the administration of the sacraments” in the old canon law to the section “offenses against the unity of the church” in the new canon law. 6.2.3. conclusion we can therefore see that npewb is not per se divine law. it is divine law only insofar as it denies the full and universal jurisdictional power of the pope, but this is not per se the case with an episcopal consecration; it is the case only when the episcopal office comes with jurisdictional power. in the case of the fsspx, however, these are mere auxiliary bishops who arrogate no jurisdictional power to themselves. thus their consecration is not a violation of divine law, but only of ecclesiastical positive law, and it can be right under the justificatory grounds listed above. 6.3. are illicit episcopal consecrations not automatically schismatic? the claim that illicit episcopal consecrations are schismatic rests partly on the false understanding refuted above, namely that jurisdictional power necessarily accompanies consecration. but the claim also rests partly on the belief that schism is constituted by wanting to withdraw from the pope’s jurisdiction, not only by arrogating it to oneself or failing to recognize it. this thesis is maintained by father bisig of the fraternity of st. peter (fssp). he writes:[88] “schism occurs when consecrations are made with the intention of withdrawing from pontifical jurisdiction or from communion of the universal church.” but this understanding of schism is simply false. raoul naz writes: original: “das schisma [...] setzt eine systematische und habituelle weigerung der abhangigkeit voraus. der ungehorsam ist oft nur eine vorubergehende handlung, ohne dass ihr urheber in irgendeiner weise die autoritat des gesetzes oder des gesetzgebers bestreitet und sich ihr auf habituelle weise entziehen will.” translation: “schism [...] presupposes a systematic and habitual refusal of dependence. disobedience is often only a passing act, without its author in any way disputing the authority of the law or of the lawgiver or wishing to withdraw from it habitually.” ( dictionnaire de droit canonique , paris: letouzey et ane, 1965, vol. vii, col. 886, quoted in [89]) st. thomas writes:[90] “the essence of schism consists in rebelliously disobeying the commandments: and i say”rebelliously,” since a schismatic both obstinately scorns the commandments of the church, and refuses to submit to her judgment.” and:[91] original: “zum zweiten punkt ist zu sagen, dass schisma eine spaltung bedeutet, die der einheit der liebe entgegensteht: denn schismatiker sind jene, die keine harmonie in den brauchen der kirche wahren, wie etwa den gehorsam gegenuber den pralaten der kirche, und die eine eigene kirche fur sich errichten wollen: und diese haben nicht von anfang an eine perverse lehre, sondern weichen vom fundament der kirche ab, wenden sich eitlem gerede zu, erfinden allerlei verirrungen und gleiten so schliesslich in die haresie ab; daher sagt hieronymus, dass sich haresie und schisma wie gattung und art unterscheiden.” translation: “to the second point it must be said that schism means a division opposed to the unity of charity: for schismatics are those who do not preserve harmony in the practices of the church, such as obedience to the prelates of the church, and who want to set up a church of their own for themselves. and these do not have a perverse doctrine from the beginning, but depart from the foundation of the church, turn to vain talk, invent all kinds of errors, and thus finally slip into heresy; hence jerome says that heresy and schism differ as genus and species.” cajetan writes: original: “ungehorsam wie hartnackig auch immer konstituiert kein schisma, ausser es handelt sich um eine rebellion gegen das amt des papstes oder das der kirche, sodass man sich weigert ihm untertan zu sein, ihn als oberen anzuerkennen” translation: “disobedience, however stubborn, does not constitute schism unless it is a rebellion against the office of the pope or that of the church, such that one refuses to be subject to him and to recognize him as superior.” the fsspx does none of these things with its consecrations. it does not reject the authority of the pope in principle and does not rebel against it, but resists it only in certain cases. it does not refuse to recognize him as superior. nor does it intend to build a parallel church of its own, as is shown by the fact that it does not arrogate jurisdiction to its bishops. nor, unlike the eastern “orthodox” schismatics, has the fsspx ever slipped into heresy. that schism is based on the fundamental rejection of papal authority is implicitly admitted also by john paul ii when, after the episcopal consecrations of 1988, he writes in ecclesia dei :[92] “hence such disobedience - which implies in practice the rejection of the roman primacy - constitutes a schismatic act.” but he is wrong in assuming that such an act implies rejection of the roman primacy, as we have already discussed. 6.4. does this not result in excommunication? for this one must first know the distinction between latae sententiae and ferendae sententiae . the former is a declaratory judgment, in which it is only established that a judgment has occurred; the latter is a constitutive judgment, that is, the judge’s sentence itself constitutes the judgment. an analogy would be a judge who establishes that a person was already convicted two years ago; here he can err, because it is only the establishment of a fact. but if he says, “you are convicted,” he cannot err, since his statement itself is the judgment. 6.4.1. the excommunications of 1988 the offense on which the vatican decree relied was canon 1382 cic 1983, today canon 1387:[93] original: “ein bischof, der jemanden ohne papstlichen auftrag zum bischof weiht, und ebenso, wer von ihm die weihe empfangt, ziehen sich die dem apostolischen stuhl vorbehaltene exkommunikation als tatstrafe zu.” translation: “a bishop who consecrates someone a bishop without a pontifical mandate, and likewise the person who receives the consecration from him, incurs a latae sententiae excommunication reserved to the apostolic see.” the declaratory decree of cardinal gantin of july 1, 1988 reads in its english original: “i declare that the above-mentioned monsignor marcel lefebvre, and bernard fellay, bernard tissier de mallerais, richard williamson and alfonso de galarreta have incurred ipso facto excommunication latae sententiae reserved to the apostolic see.” the verb “have incurred” is declaratory, not constitutive. john paul ii formulates it similarly in the motu proprio ecclesia dei of july 2, 1988:[94] original: “sind msgr. lefebvre und die priester bernard fellay, bernard tissier de mallerais, richard williamson und alfonso de galarreta der schweren strafe der exkommunikation verfallen, wie die kirchliche disziplin vorsieht.” translation: “msgr. lefebvre and the priests bernard fellay, bernard tissier de mallerais, richard williamson, and alfonso de galarreta have incurred the grave penalty of excommunication, as ecclesiastical discipline provides.” precisely this declaratory character is the starting point of the canonical defense. canon 1323 cic 1983 provides:[95] original: “keiner strafe unterworfen ist, wer bei ubertretung eines gesetzes oder eines verwaltungsbefehls: [...] 4° aus schwerer furcht, wenngleich nur relativ schwer, gezwungen oder aufgrund einer notlage oder erheblicher beschwernis gehandelt hat, sofern jedoch die tat nicht in sich schlecht ist oder zum schaden der seelen gereicht; [...] 7° ohne verschulden geglaubt hat, einen der in nn. 4 oder 5 genannten umstande liege vor.” translation: “no one is subject to a penalty who, when violating a law or administrative precept: [...] 4° was forced by grave fear, even if only relatively grave, or acted by reason of necessity or grave inconvenience, provided however that the act is not intrinsically evil or harmful to souls; [...] 7° without fault believed that one of the circumstances mentioned in nn. 4 or 5 was present.” lefebvre explicitly invoked precisely these norms for the consecrations and quoted an opinion by prof. georg may, president of the canon law seminar at the university of mainz:[96] “thus you will find among these flyers which are put at your disposal, an admirable study done by professor georg may [...] who marvelously explains why we are in a case of necessity: necessity to come and help your souls, to help you!” the necessity to which lefebvre refers can be named concretely: he expected his imminent death and had the impression that the vatican was deliberately delaying consent to an episcopal consecration until after his death in order to bring the sspx back under the influence of pro-conciliar forces afterward. this conviction at least fulfills the element of relatively grave fear in the sense of canon 1323 n. 4. whether this assessment is objectively correct is, however, secondary for the canonical question, since canon 1323 n. 7 already establishes unculpable error about the existence of the state of necessity as a complete ground excluding penalty. canon 1324 §1 n. 8 goes even further, according to which the penalty is diminished for one:[97] original: “der irrtumlich, wenngleich schuldhaft, geglaubt hat, es lage einer der in can. 1323, nn. 4 oder 5 genannten umstande vor.” translation: “who erroneously, even if culpably, believed that one of the circumstances mentioned in can. 1323, nn. 4 or 5 was present.” the decisive step follows from canon 1324 §3: original: “unter den in §1 genannten umstanden trifft den tater keine tatstrafe.” translation: “in the circumstances mentioned in §1, the offender is not subject to any latae sententiae penalty.” the canonical commentary on this passage states:[98] “§3 articulates a general principle that every diminution of imputability frees from latae sententiae penalties otherwise demanding full imputability.” since every mitigating ground of canon 1324 §1 automatically excludes every latae sententiae penalty according to §3, and since canon 1323 n. 7 qualifies unculpable error and canon 1324 §1 n. 8 even culpable error about the existence of a state of necessity as sufficient, the legal conclusion is this: even if no objective state of necessity existed, lefebvre and the four bishops incurred no latae sententiae penalty as long as they were subjectively convinced of a state of necessity without bad faith. the american canonist fr. gerard murray, whose licentiate thesis at the pontifical gregorian university received the highest grade, comes to the conclusion that the latae sententiae excommunication against lefebvre, de castro mayer, and the four bishops was “not valid according to strict canonical law,” and that the associated accusation of schism was “not valid in the formal sense.”[99] 6.4.2. ferendae sententiae excommunication but what if the fsspx bishops are excommunicated ferendae sententiae in 2026? if the justification of the fsspx that i have defended up to this point is correct, then that would simply be an unjust, though valid, judgment. the recognized dictionnaire de theologie catholique writes: original: „die theologen des mittelalters, wenigstens die des 14., 15. und 16. jahrhunderts, tragen sorge festzustellen, dass das schisma eine illegitime trennung von der kirche ist; denn, so sagen sie, es konnte auch eine legitime trennung geben, so wenn etwa jemand dem papst den gehorsam verweigerte, weil dieser ihm eine schlechte oder ungehorige sache befohle [...] die uberlegung mag uberflussig erscheinen, und man kann denken, dass hier, wie im fall der ungerechten exkommunikation, eine rein aussere und scheinbare trennung von der einheit vorliegt.“ translation: “the theologians of the middle ages, at least those of the fourteenth, fifteenth, and sixteenth centuries, take care to establish that schism is an illegitimate separation from the church; for, they say, there could also be a legitimate separation, as for example if someone refused obedience to the pope because the pope commanded him to do something bad or improper [...] the reflection may seem superfluous, and one may think that here, as in the case of unjust excommunication, there is a purely external and apparent separation from unity.” (quoted in 2. vatikanisches
